title: Nobody will tell you your idea is bad, so ask differently
description: Why direct opinion-asking produces false positives, and the specific question shapes that get past politeness to something you can actually act on.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why direct opinions about an idea are unreliable evidence
Reframe a pitch-shaped question into a behaviour-shaped one
Distinguish genuine enthusiasm from polite encouragement in a real response

contentSections.body: You show your cousin a mockup of an app that tracks freelance invoices across clients. She says "oh that's so cool, I'd totally use that!" You never hear from her again, and she never mentions it, even when you follow up two months later, still unbuilt, to ask if she'd tried anything like it yet.

contentSections.scenario:
You ask two people the same question about your invoice-tracking idea, worded two different ways.

**To Person A**, you say: "I'm thinking of building a tool that tracks freelance invoices across clients — what do you think?"

**To Person B**, you say: "How do you currently keep track of which clients owe you money and how much?"
contentSections.question: Which question is more likely to get you evidence you can act on?

options.label: The first question, to Person A
The second question, to Person B
Both equally, since they're about the same topic

feedback.a: "What do you think?" invites an opinion about your idea, and opinions about other people's ideas are cheap to give and socially costly to criticize — most people default to encouragement, which feels like validation and isn't.
feedback.b: Right. Asking how someone currently handles the problem gets you a factual answer about their actual behavior, regardless of how they feel about your idea. If they say "I just remember it, it's fine," that tells you something real. If they describe a messy multi-step workaround, that also tells you something real — and neither answer depended on being polite to you.
feedback.both: They're not equivalent. The first asks for an opinion about a hypothetical thing you made, which people soften almost automatically. The second asks about something that already happened — their actual current behavior — which is much harder to be politely vague about.

contentSections.concept: **Ask about behavior that already happened, not opinions about a thing that doesn't exist yet.** A hypothetical is easy to be nice about. A description of what someone actually does today is much harder to fake enthusiasm for, because there's nothing to be enthusiastic about — it's just a fact.

contentSections.body:
This isn't about people being dishonest. Telling a friend their idea sounds bad, to their face, while they're excited about it, is socially expensive — most people would rather offer a vague compliment and move on than run the numbers on whether they'd actually pay for something. That's not a character flaw in your friends and colleagues; it's just what politeness costs, and it means their opinion of your idea is systematically inflated compared to their actual future behavior.

The practical result: **treat every unprompted "I'd totally use that" as worth zero, on its own**, until it's backed by something the person actually did — described a real current workaround, agreed to a specific next step (a call, an email when it's ready, testing an early version), or, best of all, is already paying for something adjacent that solves part of the same problem.
"I'd use that" is free to say and costs nothing to be wrong about. Ask about what someone already does, not what they'd hypothetically do.

contentSections.title: Reading the response you actually got

contentSections.body: You ask a former coworker how he tracks invoices. He spends four minutes describing, in specific and slightly irritated detail, a system involving three spreadsheets and a recurring calendar reminder he usually ignores. That's a completely different kind of response than "oh, I use an app for that, works fine."

contentSections.scenario: You've asked five people the behavior-based question from this lesson. Here are their responses.
contentSections.question: Which of these responses count as genuine signal worth logging as a strong candidate? Select all that apply.

items.label: A four-minute, specific, slightly irritated description of a multi-step manual workaround
"I use [existing tool], works fine" — said quickly, no further detail offered
"Actually, could I try whatever you build? I'd genuinely pay to not do this anymore"
"Yeah I guess that's kind of annoying," said flatly, with no example
"I lost track of an invoice for six weeks last month because of this exact thing"

explanation.detailed-complaint: Length and specificity are themselves a signal — people don't spend four minutes describing something in irritated detail unless it's actually costing them something. Vague responses take five seconds; this one didn't.
explanation.quick-fine: "Works fine," said quickly with nothing added, usually means exactly what it says: they have already solved this well enough that it's not worth more of their attention. That's useful information — it points away from this idea, not toward it.
explanation.unprompted-offer: An unprompted offer to pay, or to be a test user, is about as strong as pre-product signal gets — it's the person volunteering a costly commitment, not you extracting a compliment.
explanation.vague-yes: Flat agreement with no example attached is close to the "I'd totally use that" pattern from earlier — cheap to say, no real content behind it.
explanation.specific-cost: A specific, dated, costed incident ("lost track of an invoice for six weeks") is concrete evidence of real damage, not a feeling — exactly the kind of detail a polite non-answer never includes.

contentSections.synthesis: The shape to watch for isn't whether someone sounds positive — it's whether they hand you a specific detail, a real cost, or a real commitment, unprompted. Vague answers, positive or negative, are equally uninformative.

contentSections.body: One trap worth naming directly: a detailed, irritated description of a workaround is strong signal about the *problem* — it is not automatically a promise that this specific person would use *your* solution. Keep those two facts separate in your notes. "This is a real, costly problem for them" and "they would switch to what I build" are different claims, and only the first one is something a single conversation can really establish.
Specificity, cost and unprompted commitment are signal. Speed and vagueness — even friendly vagueness — are not.

title: Asking about behaviour, not about intentions
description: The gap between what people say they'd do and what they actually do, and the question templates that ask about the past instead of the future.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why stated future intentions are weaker evidence than past behaviour
Convert an intention-shaped question into a behaviour-shaped one

contentSections.title: The gap between saying and doing

contentSections.body: "Would you pay $10/month for a tool that does X?" Almost everyone says yes to this question, for almost any X, because saying yes costs nothing right now and imagining a future $10 charge feels abstract and easy to accept.

contentSections.scenario: A founder surveys 200 people: "would you use a tool that automatically categorizes your business receipts for tax season?" 78% say yes. She builds it. Six months later, fewer than 2% of the people who said yes have signed up.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism behind this gap?

options.label: The 200 people lied on the survey
A future intention costs nothing to state and doesn't compete with anything else in their life the way an actual switch would
The product just wasn't built well enough

feedback.lied: Most people weren't lying — in the moment of answering, they probably did imagine they'd use it. The problem is what "imagining using it" costs versus what actually adopting a new tool costs.
feedback.cost: Right. Saying yes to a hypothetical costs nothing — no time, no habit change, no decision about which existing tool to drop. Actually switching to a new tool competes with inertia, existing habits, and every other thing on their plate. The survey question never tested that competition; it just tested whether the idea sounded reasonable.
feedback.quality: Maybe the product had flaws, but 2% adoption from 78% stated interest is a gap so large that build quality alone can't explain it — this pattern shows up even for well-built products tested this way.

contentSections.mechanism: **A stated future intention isn't weighed against anything.** It doesn't have to fight your existing habits, your subscription fatigue, or the ten other tools already open on your desktop — because none of those costs are present in the moment of answering a hypothetical question. Only actual behavior carries that competition built in.

contentSections.body:
The fix isn't to distrust everyone — it's to ask questions that are actually about the past, where the competition already happened and a real answer already exists. A short set of reliable conversions:

| Instead of asking... | Ask... |
|---|---|
| "Would you use X?" | "What do you currently do about [the problem X solves]?" |
| "Would you pay for X?" | "What are you paying for right now to deal with this, if anything?" |
| "Would this save you time?" | "How much time did you spend on this last week, specifically?" |
| "Is this a priority for you?" | "When's the last time you actually tried to fix this yourself?" |

Each right-hand question can only be answered by describing something that already happened — there's no room for a costless hypothetical yes.
A future intention is free to state. Ask what someone already did — that's the only version of the question with real cost baked in.

You ask a small business owner what she currently pays for expense tracking. She says "nothing, I just use a shoebox of receipts." That sounds like zero investment — and zero investment can look like zero pain, which would be the wrong read here.

contentSections.question: The shoebox-of-receipts answer sounds like "no current spend, so no real problem." What question would you ask next to find out if that's true?
contentSections.answer: Something like: "What happens with that shoebox at tax time?" or "Has that shoebox ever caused a problem — a missed deduction, a stressful scramble, a fight with an accountant?" The absence of a paid tool doesn't mean the absence of cost; it might mean the cost is paid later, in a lump, in a way that's easy to not connect back to the shoebox.
contentSections.hint: Zero dollars spent isn't the same as zero cost — the cost might just be deferred, or paid in a currency other than money (time, stress, mistakes).

contentSections.body: Behavior questions are much stronger than intention questions, but they still have a failure mode: a "no current spend" or "I don't really do anything about it" answer can mean genuinely no problem, or it can mean the cost is invisible, deferred, or paid by someone else. The follow-up that separates the two is almost always the same shape: *what happens when this goes wrong, and when did it last happen?* A shoebox with no story attached to it is different from a shoebox that caused a stressful three-hour scramble every April.
Zero current spend isn't the same as zero cost. Follow up on what happens when the workaround fails, not just whether one exists.

title: The existing solution people already put up with
description: Taking a competitor's or a workaround's shortcomings seriously as a validation source, and the difference between disliking a tool and being willing to leave it.

learningObjectives.text: Use complaints about an existing solution as validation evidence
Distinguish dissatisfaction from switching willingness

contentSections.body: You want to build a simpler expense-report tool. Instead of asking anyone whether they'd use yours, you spend twenty minutes reading the one-star and two-star reviews of the three most popular existing expense tools. By review twelve, the same three complaints are repeating almost word for word.

contentSections.question: Put these steps of reading competitor reviews for validation in the order that gets you the most reliable signal.
steps: Find the two or three most-used existing tools in the category
Read the low-star reviews specifically, not the average-star ones
Note which specific complaints repeat across multiple independent reviewers
Check whether the repeated complaint is about something core (the tool doesn't solve the actual problem) or peripheral (a preference about button color)
Treat only the repeated, core complaints as validated demand for something better
contentSections.explanation: Low-star reviews are where people who were frustrated enough to write something took the time to write it — that's a much higher bar than a survey response. Repetition across independent reviewers is what separates a real gap from one person's pet peeve, and separating core from peripheral complaints is what keeps you from building a whole tool to fix a button color.

contentSections.body:
This works because people who already tried the mainstream solution and are still unhappy enough to leave a public complaint have already paid the cost your survey question can't measure — they adopted something, used it for real, and it still didn't solve their problem. That's much stronger evidence than a hypothetical "would you use a better version."

The same logic works on workarounds people describe to you directly, not just public reviews: someone who's already tried the leading tool in your category, found it lacking, and gone back to a spreadsheet has told you something a cold survey response never could — the existing options were evaluated and rejected, specifically.
A repeated complaint about an existing tool, from people who already tried it, is stronger validation than a hypothetical about yours.

contentSections.title: Disliking it isn't the same as leaving it

contentSections.body: A project manager tells you, at length, everything wrong with the tool his company uses. Then you ask if he'd switch to something better, and he says "honestly, probably not — getting twelve people retrained would be a nightmare, and it mostly works."

contentSections.scenario:
Two people complain about their current tool.

**Person A** is a solo freelancer who complains about her invoicing app, then adds: "if something simpler existed I'd switch tomorrow, I already looked."

**Person B** is a project manager at a 40-person company who complains at length about the project tracker, then says switching would mean retraining the whole team and he doesn't have the authority to decide anyway.
contentSections.question: Which complaint is closer to being validated demand you could act on?

options.label: Person A's
Person B's
Both equally — they're both frustrated

feedback.a: Right. Person A has both the pain and the authority and stated willingness to act on it — she can switch tomorrow, on her own, and says she would. That's demand you could actually convert.
feedback.b: Person B's frustration is real, but he's told you directly that switching costs (retraining) and lack of authority (it's not his call) stand between his complaint and any action. Building for him alone, based on this complaint, ignores the two things he just told you would stop him.
feedback.both: The frustration is comparable, but the path from complaint to action is completely different — one person can act unilaterally and says she would, the other has named two specific blockers to ever switching regardless of how good your tool is.

contentSections.concept: **Dissatisfaction plus the authority and stated willingness to switch is demand. Dissatisfaction alone is just dissatisfaction.** Always ask, after a complaint: could this person actually switch if something better existed, and would switching costs eat the entire benefit?

contentSections.body: A complaint only becomes validated demand once you know the person could actually act on it — has the authority, and switching costs wouldn't cancel out the benefit.

title: Cheap signals: a landing page, a post, a waitlist
description: Testing demand with an artefact that costs an afternoon instead of a build that costs a month, and reading the resulting numbers honestly.

learningObjectives.text: Design a cheap pre-build signal test appropriate to an idea
Interpret a signal test's results without over- or under-reading them

contentSections.title: An afternoon instead of a month

contentSections.body: Instead of building the invoice tracker, you spend an afternoon writing one paragraph describing it, putting it on a single page with an email field, and posting the link in two communities you're a real member of. By the end of the week: 34 visits, 6 emails.

contentSections.intro: Assemble a cheap signal test for the invoice-tracker idea from earlier in the module — a landing page plus a waitlist, posted where real potential users already are.

fields.prompt: What should the landing page actually contain?
options: One clear paragraph describing the specific problem it solves, and one field to collect an email
A full feature list and pricing tiers, so people know exactly what they're signing up for
A polished demo video and a countdown timer to create urgency
fields.correctValue: One clear paragraph describing the specific problem it solves, and one field to collect an email
fields.feedback: A landing page for this stage is testing one thing — does the problem description resonate enough that someone hands over an email. A feature list and pricing tiers describe a product you haven't built and haven't validated yet; a countdown timer manufactures urgency that has nothing to do with real demand.

fields.prompt: Where should you post the link?
options: Communities you're a genuine, already-active member of, where the problem is relevant
As many places as possible, to maximize total traffic
Only to close friends, to guarantee a warm response
fields.correctValue: Communities you're a genuine, already-active member of, where the problem is relevant
fields.feedback: Traffic from people who don't have the problem tells you nothing — it just inflates a visit count. Close friends are also the group most likely to click out of politeness rather than genuine need. The useful signal comes from real potential users, which is exactly who's in the community you're already part of.

fields.prompt: What's the number that actually matters here?
options: The ratio of emails collected to relevant visits, not the raw visit count
Total page visits, regardless of source
How many likes or reactions the post got
fields.correctValue: The ratio of emails collected to relevant visits, not the raw visit count
fields.feedback: Raw visits and reactions can both be inflated by curiosity or algorithm luck and say nothing about real demand. The conversion ratio — how many of the people who actually saw the specific problem description handed over an email — is what approximates a real willingness-to-act signal.

contentSections.synthesis: A specific problem statement, posted to people who genuinely have the problem, measured by conversion rather than raw traffic — that's the whole test, and it costs an afternoon instead of a month.

contentSections.body: A cheap signal test answers one question — does the problem description convert real potential users into a real action — and nothing more.

34 visits, 6 emails. Is that good? On its own, the number means almost nothing — a 17% conversion rate could be excellent or could be six polite friends clicking a link, depending entirely on who those 34 visitors actually were.

contentSections.scenario: You post your landing page in a community of active freelancers where the invoice-tracking problem is genuinely relevant, and get 34 visits from people you don't personally know.
contentSections.question: Roughly what email-conversion rate from a well-targeted, cold (non-friend) audience like this would you consider a real, actionable signal worth pursuing?
contentSections.explanation: There's no single universal number, but a rough, honest rule of thumb for a well-targeted cold audience: somewhere around 8-15% starts to look like a real signal worth a next step; below roughly 3-5% from a genuinely relevant, non-friend audience is usually a sign the problem statement isn't resonating, or the problem itself isn't as sharp as you thought. What matters far more than hitting an exact number is knowing who the visitors actually were — a high rate from six friends means much less than a lower rate from thirty strangers who found it relevant enough to click through on their own.

contentSections.body: The honest reading of any signal test requires knowing the denominator, not just the headline number. "6 emails" sounds like validation. "6 emails, and 3 of the 34 visits were my mom, my roommate, and a coworker who felt obligated" is a different, much weaker result. Before you trust a conversion number, ask: how many of these visitors were strangers with the actual problem, versus people clicking to be nice? Only the first group's behavior is real signal.
A conversion number only means something once you know who was in the denominator — strangers with the problem, or friends being nice.

title: Killing an idea early and cheaply
description: Recognizing when the evidence says stop, and treating a killed idea as a cheap, useful outcome instead of a failure to push through.

learningObjectives.text: Recognize the evidence patterns that call for killing an idea before building
Distinguish a genuine kill signal from ordinary discouragement worth pushing through

contentSections.title: What a kill signal actually looks like

contentSections.body: You talked to eleven people about the invoice tracker. Nine described a workaround they were fine with. Two had a real complaint but no authority to switch tools at their company. Nobody, unprompted, asked to try anything. You've spent four hours finding this out, not four months.

contentSections.scenario: You're reviewing everything you've learned about the invoice tracker across this module's validation methods.
contentSections.question: Which of these, taken together, would genuinely justify killing the idea at this stage? Select all that apply.

items.label: Most people describe a workaround with no specific cost or frustration attached to it
The people with the strongest complaints don't have the authority to switch tools themselves
One person you asked said no
Nobody, across every conversation, volunteered a next step or asked to try anything
Building it stopped sounding exciting to you personally

explanation.no-cost: This is close to the module's core test failing directly — no nameable cost was the whole thing lesson one was checking for, and it's showing up as absent across most conversations, not just one.
explanation.no-authority: If the people who feel the pain most can't act on it, that's a structural blocker independent of how good your tool ends up being — this is the authority-to-switch problem from lesson three.
explanation.one-rejection: A single no is just one data point, and one data point out of many conversations doesn't override everything else you've learned. This one alone shouldn't move the decision.
explanation.no-commitment: Zero unprompted commitments across every conversation is a real pattern, not noise — this is exactly the kind of behavior-based evidence lesson one said to look for, and its absence is informative.
explanation.not-fun: Personal enthusiasm dipping is worth noticing about yourself, but it's not evidence about the market — plenty of things worth building go through unmotivated stretches, and this shouldn't be treated as validation data.

contentSections.synthesis: Kill decisions should rest on patterns across multiple conversations, not a single rejection or your own mood — but when several of those patterns line up together, that's exactly the evidence this module has been teaching you to collect.

contentSections.body: The reason this is worth teaching explicitly is that killing an idea feels like failure, so people avoid reading the evidence that says to do it. It isn't a failure — it's the fastest, cheapest possible outcome of this whole module. Four hours of honest conversations that end in "this doesn't hold up" is a good result, not a bad one, compared to the alternative: four months of building something the same four hours of conversation would have ruled out.
A pattern across many conversations — not one rejection, not your own dip in motivation — is what justifies a kill. When it's there, killing early is a win, not a loss.

contentSections.title: What to do with a killed idea

contentSections.body: The invoice tracker is dead. But three of those eleven conversations mentioned, almost in passing, a completely different problem: none of them could find a simple way to split a project's expenses with a subcontractor. That's a new log entry, not a wasted afternoon.

contentSections.question: You just killed the invoice-tracker idea after eleven conversations. What's the single most useful thing to write down before moving to the next candidate in your idea log?
contentSections.answer: Specifically which evidence pattern killed it (no cost named, no authority to switch, zero unprompted commitment) — not just "didn't work out." That specificity is what makes the next validation round faster, because you'll recognize the same pattern sooner next time.
contentSections.hint: Think about what would make your next validation attempt faster, not just what closes out this one.

contentSections.body: A killed idea rarely means the four hours were wasted — it usually means you learned something specific about a market you were previously guessing about, and picked up at least one adjacent friction along the way, per the idea-log habit from module one. Before moving on, it's worth writing down, briefly: what exactly killed it (which of the patterns from this lesson showed up), and what you noticed in passing that might be worth its own entry.
A killed idea that taught you the specific pattern that killed it, and handed you one adjacent lead, was four hours well spent.

title: Design a validation test for seven ideas
description: Seven drills on the module's skills — reframing questions, reading responses honestly, and reading a signal test's numbers correctly.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the module's question-reframing and evidence-reading skills to unfamiliar scenarios
Recognize genuine kill and go signals under time pressure

contentSections.body: Seven drills across this module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Nothing here is timed or expires — do it in one sitting or spread out.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Validate one idea before writing code
description: Take one real candidate from your idea log and actually run it through behavior-based questions with real people before building anything.

learningObjectives.text: Design and run real behavior-based validation conversations
Reach and record an honest go/no-go decision from the evidence

contentSections.body: Pick one candidate from the idea log you built last module — or, if you don't have one yet, one real friction from your own recent work. This lab only works with a real idea and real people; there's no substitute version that uses invented data.

contentSections.title: Your validation record
contentSections.brief: You have one candidate idea. Before you write a line of code for it, find out — using this module's tools — whether it's actually wanted. This lab produces a real document: what you asked, who answered, and your honest go/no-go call.
contentSections.deliverable: A validation record with what you asked, who answered and what they said, and a go/no-go decision with the specific evidence behind it.

stages.title: Write your behavior-based questions
stages.instructions: Write two or three questions about your candidate idea, using the reframing from lesson two: about current behavior, not future intention. Then write one likely follow-up for a "no current spend" or "nothing, really" answer, per lesson two's second half.
stages.checkpoint: You have questions that ask about the past, not the future, plus one follow-up for a flat or vague first answer.

stages.title: Talk to at least five real people
stages.instructions: Ask your questions to at least five real people who plausibly have this problem — not close friends only, and not made-up composites. Write down what each person actually said, as close to their own words as you can get, immediately after each conversation. Note anything unprompted: a request to try it, a specific cost mentioned, a flat no.
stages.checkpoint: You have notes from at least five real conversations, in the other person's own words where possible, not summarized into your own paraphrase.

stages.title: Reach and record a go/no-go decision
stages.instructions: Reread your five-plus conversations against this module's evidence patterns: nameable cost, authority to switch, unprompted commitment. Write your decision — go, no-go, or "need three more conversations to tell" — and name the specific evidence that drove it, not a general impression.
stages.checkpoint: Your decision names specific evidence from specific conversations, and could be defended to someone who wasn't in the room.

rubric.criterion: Questions are behavior-based, not intention-based
rubric.meets: Every question asks about something that already happened, per the conversion table in lesson two.

rubric.criterion: Conversations are with real people, not composites
rubric.meets: At least five real, distinct people, not close-friends-only, with notes close to their actual words.

rubric.criterion: The record distinguishes strong signal from polite noise
rubric.meets: Notes flag which responses had specificity, cost, or unprompted commitment versus which were vague or fast.

rubric.criterion: The decision is evidence-based, not vibes-based
rubric.meets: The go/no-go call cites specific things specific people said, not a general sense of how it went.

rubric.criterion: A no-go, if reached, is treated as a real result
rubric.meets: If the evidence says kill it, the record says so plainly, with what was learned, rather than being stretched into a go.

rubric.criterion: It's a document your future self could act on
rubric.meets: Someone reading only this record, with no other context, would understand what was asked, who answered, and why the decision landed where it did.

contentSections.body: Five real conversations, honestly recorded, beat a hundred hypothetical yeses — and a clean no-go here is worth exactly as much as a clean go.

title: Checkpoint — Finding Out Before You Build
description: Ten questions, half from this module, half from the previous one. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's and the previous module's core distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Checkpoint — Finding Out Before You Build

questions.from: This module — Finding Out Before You Build
questions.prompt: Why is "what do you think?" a weak validation question?

options.label: It invites an opinion about a hypothetical, which is cheap to be nice about
People always lie when asked directly
It's too short to get a useful answer

questions.explanation: The problem isn't dishonesty — it's that an opinion about something hypothetical costs the responder nothing, so politeness fills in the gap. Asking about behavior that already happened removes that cheap escape route.

questions.from: This module — Finding Out Before You Build
questions.prompt: Why do stated future intentions ("would you pay for X?") produce inflated yes rates?

options.label: A hypothetical yes doesn't have to compete with real switching costs and existing habits
Survey respondents are paid to say yes
The questions are usually worded confusingly

questions.explanation: Nothing in the moment of answering a hypothetical forces the responder to weigh it against their actual habits, subscriptions, or attention — that competition only shows up when a real switch is actually on the table.

questions.from: This module — Finding Out Before You Build
questions.prompt: Someone says "nothing, I just use a shoebox of receipts" when asked what they currently pay for expense tracking. What should you do next?

options.label: Ask what happens with that shoebox when something goes wrong, since zero spend isn't the same as zero cost
Conclude there's no problem and move on
Assume they're not a serious enough business to be a target user

questions.explanation: Zero current spend can mean no problem, or it can mean the cost is deferred or invisible — the follow-up about what happens when it fails is what tells the two apart.

questions.from: This module — Finding Out Before You Build
questions.prompt: Why are low-star reviews of an existing competitor a strong validation source?

options.label: The reviewers already adopted and used a real solution, and it still didn't solve their problem
Low-star reviews are always accurate
They're free to read

questions.explanation: These reviewers paid the real cost of adopting a mainstream tool and are still frustrated — that's stronger evidence than a hypothetical about a tool that doesn't exist yet, because they already did the thing your survey question can only imagine.

questions.from: This module — Finding Out Before You Build
questions.prompt: A project manager complains at length about his team's tool, then says switching would mean retraining twelve people and isn't his call anyway. What does his complaint represent?

options.label: Dissatisfaction without the authority or ability to act on it — not yet validated demand
Strong validated demand, since the complaint was detailed
Evidence the tool itself is badly built

questions.explanation: Demand requires both pain and the ability to act on it. A detailed complaint from someone who's told you directly he can't or won't switch is real frustration, but it isn't demand you could convert.

questions.from: This module — Finding Out Before You Build
questions.prompt: What should a cheap landing-page signal test actually measure?

options.label: The conversion rate among relevant, non-friend visitors, not raw visit count
Total page visits from any source
How many likes the announcement post got

questions.explanation: Raw traffic and reactions can be inflated by curiosity, algorithms, or friends being nice. The conversion rate among people who genuinely have the problem is what approximates real demand.

questions.from: This module — Finding Out Before You Build
questions.prompt: Which pattern, seen across many conversations, would genuinely justify killing an idea?

options.label: No nameable cost, no authority to switch, and zero unprompted commitment, repeated across most conversations
One person out of many said no
You personally stopped feeling excited about it

questions.explanation: A single no, or a dip in your own motivation, is a data point, not a pattern. Several structural signals lining up across many conversations is what the module's evidence-reading was built to catch.

questions.from: This module — Finding Out Before You Build
questions.prompt: Why treat a killed idea as a good outcome rather than a failure?

options.label: A few hours of honest conversation is far cheaper than months of building something the same conversations would have ruled out
Killed ideas can always be revived later with no cost
It proves you're being appropriately cautious as a founder

questions.explanation: The whole point of validating cheaply is that the worst case — the idea doesn't hold up — costs a few hours instead of a few months. That's the win being described, not caution for its own sake.

questions.from: The previous module — Where Ideas Actually Come From
questions.prompt: What makes an annoyance a trustworthy signal rather than a thin preference?

options.label: It repeats on a schedule, has a nameable cost, and a structural cause
It's the most dramatic thing that's happened to you this month
Other people would find it funny if you complained about it

questions.explanation: Repetition, a nameable cost, and a structural cause together are what separate a real signal from a mild taste — the same shape of evidence this module asks you to look for in other people's answers, not just your own annoyances.

questions.from: The previous module — Where Ideas Actually Come From
questions.prompt: What's the first question worth asking the owner of a strained, fragile spreadsheet?

options.label: What does one row represent?
How many tabs does this have?
How long have you used spreadsheets?

questions.explanation: "What does one row represent" surfaces the core entity a v1 tool would need to model. It's the same instinct as this module's behavior-based questions — ask about something concrete and already real, not a generic preference.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: The version that's useful in one week
description: Scoping to a fixed, small time budget forces the real question — what's the smallest thing that's actually useful, not just the smallest thing that's technically possible.

learningObjectives.text: Use a fixed time budget as a scoping constraint rather than an afterthought
Distinguish 'smallest possible' from 'smallest useful'

contentSections.title: Small isn't the same as useful

contentSections.body: You validated the invoice tracker — five real conversations, a genuine repeated cost, two people who'd switch tomorrow. Now you open a blank editor and, out of habit, start sketching a database schema with clients, invoices, line items, tax rates, currencies, and recurring billing. None of the five people you talked to mentioned currencies.

contentSections.scenario:
Two different "smallest versions" of the same validated invoice tracker.

**Version A** does one thing: takes a list of invoices with amounts and due dates, and tells you which are overdue. No editing, no client database, just a flat list and a status.

**Version B** is a stripped-down clone of a real invoicing app — client records, editable invoices, PDF export, all with a smaller feature set than the leading tools.
contentSections.question: Which is more likely to be genuinely useful in one week of work?

options.label: Version A
Version B
Neither — a week is never enough for a real tool

feedback.a: Right. Version A does exactly one job — telling you what's overdue — completely, using data the person already has. It's small in scope, not small in usefulness.
feedback.b: Version B is small in the sense of "fewer features than a real product," but it's still trying to be a whole category of tool at once — client records, editing, export. That shape doesn't compress into a week; it just becomes a worse, half-finished version of the same big thing.
feedback.neither: A week is a real constraint, not an excuse — Version A is a complete, genuinely useful thing at that size. The mistake isn't the time budget; it's reaching for a miniature clone of a big tool instead of a small tool that does one job all the way through.

contentSections.concept: **"Smallest possible" usually means fewer features of a big idea. "Smallest useful" means one complete job, done all the way through, using what the person already has.** The second one is what actually fits in a week — the first one just fits worse.

contentSections.body:
A fixed, honest time budget is a scoping tool, not a compromise you're forced into. Without one, almost every idea quietly expands to "a smaller version of everything the market leader does," because that's the shape your brain defaults to when it thinks about a category of product. With a real deadline in front of you — one week, for real, not "a week, ish" — the only way to hit it is to ask a completely different question: **what's the one job, done completely, that would already be useful on day one?**

This matters especially for anyone building around variable energy and unpredictable good days: a scope that assumes a month of steady effort is a scope that dies the first time a bad week happens. A scope that's genuinely a week of work survives a bad week — you just ship it the following week instead.
A fixed time budget forces the real question: not "how do I make the big idea smaller," but "what's the one job I can finish completely."

Every version of the invoice tracker you've sketched so far assumes people will type their invoices into your tool. But every single person you validated with already has their invoices somewhere — a spreadsheet, an email thread, an existing tool's export. Building a place to re-type them is the first thing to cut.

contentSections.scenario: You're scoping the invoice tracker to one week. Here are candidate v1 decisions.
contentSections.question: Which of these choices genuinely shrink the build to something a week can hold? Select all that apply.

items.label: Accept a CSV export of what people already track, instead of building data entry
Build for one person's invoices at a time, no team accounts or permissions yet
Use a simpler color palette in the UI
Track exactly one status — overdue or not — instead of a full lifecycle (draft, sent, paid, overdue, disputed)
Use text labels instead of custom icons

explanation.import-csv: This removes an entire feature area — data entry, validation, editing — by using data the person already produces, which is exactly the kind of cut that changes what fits in a week.
explanation.single-user: Multi-user support brings permissions, invitations, and shared state with it — cutting it removes a whole category of complexity, not just a visual detail.
explanation.fewer-colors: This is a cosmetic choice. It might save an hour of design time, but it doesn't change the shape or size of what you're building.
explanation.one-status: This is the same move as the CSV import — instead of modeling a whole lifecycle, you model the one state (overdue) that the validated problem was actually about.
explanation.fewer-icons: Also cosmetic. Icons versus text labels doesn't touch the actual scope of the build.

contentSections.synthesis: The cuts that matter change what the tool has to model and build, not how it looks. Visual simplicity is nice; structural simplicity is what makes a week honest.

contentSections.body: "Use what they already have" is one of the most reliable one-week moves available: importing a CSV instead of building data entry, reading an existing export instead of building an integration, asking someone to paste text instead of building a rich editor. None of these are permanent decisions — they're what makes week one possible, and the next lesson is specifically about deciding which of these you're allowed to punt on and which one thing you can't.
The fastest way to shrink a build is to use data and formats people already have instead of building a way to create them from scratch.

title: One job, done completely
description: Picking the single job a v1 has to do, and the difference between doing it completely versus doing several jobs partway.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the one job a v1 must do completely
Recognize when a scope has quietly become several partial jobs instead of one complete one

contentSections.title: One job, not several partial ones

contentSections.body: A first draft of the invoice-tracker scope: import a CSV (partly working), flag overdue invoices (partly working), send a reminder email (partly working), show a dashboard chart (partly working). Four features, each about 70% done, and the tool does nothing anyone could actually rely on yet.

contentSections.scenario: Four features, each roughly 70% built, versus one feature fully built. Both took the same total number of hours. Only one is shippable.
contentSections.question: What's the actual reason four 70%-done features are worth less than one 100%-done feature, even at equal total effort?

options.label: 70% features have more bugs on average
A feature that isn't complete can't be relied on, and a tool with zero reliable features is worth nothing to a real user regardless of how much work went into it
Users prefer tools with fewer features

feedback.bugs: Bug count isn't really the mechanism — a 70% feature might have few bugs in the part that's built. The problem is what's simply missing, not what's broken.
feedback.reliability: Right. A real user needs to trust that the one thing they're using the tool for actually works, every time. Four partial features give them zero things they can trust completely — the effort was real, but none of it converted into something usable.
feedback.preference: This isn't really about preference — a tool with one complete feature and a tool with ten complete features can both work fine. The problem with four partial features isn't feature count, it's that none of them can be depended on.

contentSections.mechanism: **Usefulness comes from completeness, not from effort spent.** A user can rely on a feature that works every time. They can't rely on four features that mostly work — mostly working is functionally the same as not working, from the point of view of someone trying to depend on it.

contentSections.body:
This is why "one job, done completely" beats "several jobs, mostly done" even when the total hours are identical. The practical test: pick the one job a stranger could rely on this tool for, on day one, without you standing next to them explaining what's still rough. Everything else — the reminder email, the dashboard, the second status — waits until that one job is genuinely solid, not just started.

The hard part of this lesson usually isn't understanding it; it's actually picking the one job, because everything you've validated feels equally important in the moment. A rough filter: which job, if it were the *only* thing this tool did, would still be worth someone's time to use today?
Four features at 70% are worth less than one feature at 100% — a user can't rely on "mostly works."

contentSections.title: Picking the job from your own validation notes

contentSections.body: You reread your validation record from module two. Of the five people you talked to, all five mentioned losing track of which invoices were overdue. Two mentioned wanting reminder emails sent automatically. Nobody mentioned dashboards or charts, not once.

contentSections.scenario: You're picking the one job for the invoice tracker's v1, based on five validation conversations: five out of five mentioned losing track of overdue invoices; two of five mentioned wanting automatic reminders; zero mentioned dashboards.
contentSections.question: How many of the five conversations should independently mention something before you treat it as a strong candidate for "the one job" a v1 must do?
contentSections.explanation: There's no hard rule, but a workable one: something close to unanimous — four or five out of five — is a strong signal for the one job a v1 has to nail. Something mentioned by a minority (two of five, here) is real, but it's evidence for a fast-following v2, not for what v1 has to be built around. Zero mentions, however easy the feature would be to build, means it doesn't belong in scope at all yet — ease of building has nothing to do with whether it was validated.

contentSections.body: Your validation record is the actual source for this decision, not a fresh brainstorm. The job that showed up in every conversation — knowing which invoices are overdue — is the strongest candidate for "the one job," precisely because it's the thing that was independently, repeatedly confirmed. The job two people mentioned (automatic reminders) is real but secondary; it can wait for a version two built on top of a working v1. The thing nobody mentioned (a dashboard) doesn't belong in scope at all yet, no matter how easy it would be to add.
The one job a v1 does isn't a fresh guess — it's whatever showed up independently across nearly all of your validation conversations.

title: Features to cut, and the one you can't
description: A practical method for sorting a feature list into what waits and the single thing that has to be there for the one job to actually work.

learningObjectives.text: Sort a feature list by whether it's required for the one job or deferrable
Identify the single feature that can't be cut without breaking the core job

contentSections.body: You have a list of eleven things the invoice tracker could do. You need it down to something a week can build. Cutting by "which ones sound less exciting" gets you nowhere — everything on the list sounds at least a little useful.

contentSections.question: Put these steps of the cut test in order, from first question to last.
steps: Name the one job (from lesson two) precisely, in one sentence
For each item on the feature list, ask: does the one job still work at all without this?
If the job still works without it, mark it deferred — not deleted, just not in v1
If the job breaks without it, mark it required
Check that the required list is short — if more than two or three items are 'required,' the one job was probably defined too broadly
contentSections.explanation: The test only works once the one job is pinned down precisely — a vague job description makes everything sound required. Running the "does it still work without this" question against a precise job is what actually separates deferred from required, and the final sanity check catches the common failure mode where the job itself was scoped too big to begin with.

contentSections.body:
Applied to the invoice tracker, whose one job is *"tell someone which of their invoices are overdue, using data they already have"*:

- **CSV import** — required. Without it, there's no data, and the job can't run at all.
- **Overdue calculation** — required. This is the job itself.
- **A visible list of results** — required. If nobody can see the output, the job didn't happen.
- **Editing invoices in the tool** — deferred. The job still works if editing happens back in the spreadsheet and you just re-import.
- **Reminder emails** — deferred. The job (telling *you*) still works without automatically telling the client too.
- **Multiple currencies** — deferred, maybe permanently, unless your actual validated users need it.

Three required items, not eleven. That's what "the one job, done completely" actually looks like once you run the test against a precise job description instead of a vague one.
A feature is required only if the one job breaks without it. Everything else is deferred, not deleted.

contentSections.title: When the required list is too long

contentSections.body: You run the cut test on a different idea — a tool that helps freelancers split project expenses with subcontractors — and get seven "required" items. Something's wrong, and it isn't the test.

contentSections.title: The scope that keeps growing back
contentSections.opening: You've scoped the invoice tracker to three required features. Two days into your one-week build, a friend you're excited to show it to says: "oh, but what about invoices in a different currency? I have clients in Canada." It's a fair point, and it would only take an extra evening.

reply.situation: It's genuinely a small addition on its own. Your one week is half gone. The three required features aren't finished yet.
reply.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Add currency support now — it's small and the feedback is good
choices.consequence: Currency support takes the promised evening, plus another evening for an edge case with rounding you didn't anticipate. Your original three required features are now further from done than they were two days ago.

choices.label: Log it as a deferred item and keep building the three required features
choices.consequence: You finish the three required features on schedule. Currency support is now a clearly-named line at the top of your v2 list, with your friend's specific use case attached to it.

choices.label: Tell your friend it'll never support other currencies
choices.consequence: You've turned a reasonable, well-timed piece of feedback into a permanent no, for no real reason — currency support might genuinely matter for v2, and you didn't need to close that door to stay on schedule this week.

scope-crept.summary: One small, reasonable-sounding addition, two days before the deadline, is enough to blow a one-week scope — not because it was a bad idea, but because "small" additions rarely stay small once you're inside them.
scope-crept.lesson: The required list from the cut test exists specifically to survive moments like this. A friend's good, well-timed suggestion is still a new item being added mid-build, and "it's small" is exactly what everything sounds like from the outside, before you've hit its first edge case.

shipped.summary: The three required features ship on time. Currency support becomes a well-defined, validated v2 candidate instead of an unplanned mid-build detour.
shipped.lesson: Deferring isn't rejecting — it's the difference between "not now, and here's exactly where it goes next" and either an uncontrolled scope expansion or a hard, unnecessary no. This is the same discipline as the idea log: write it down specifically, don't lose it, don't let it derail what's already in motion.

overcorrected.summary: You protect the timeline, but at a cost you didn't need to pay — a real, validated-sounding need is now permanently off the table instead of just deferred.
overcorrected.lesson: Scoping down for a week doesn't require deciding a feature will never exist. It only requires deciding it doesn't exist yet. Confusing "not in v1" with "never" throws away real signal for no scheduling benefit.

contentSections.body: A long required list almost always means the one job from lesson two was defined too broadly, not that the idea genuinely needs seven load-bearing features. "Split project expenses with subcontractors" is really several jobs stacked together — tracking who paid what, calculating fair shares, handling disputes, generating a payout record — each with its own required list. The fix isn't to grind through cutting from all seven; it's to go back and re-narrow the one job to something like *"tell two people, given a list of shared expenses, exactly who owes whom and how much"* — and rerun the test against that.
A reasonable-sounding addition mid-build is still scope creep. "Not in v1" and "never" are different answers — use the first one, not the second.

title: Manual behind the curtain: faking the hard part
description: Doing the hardest, most uncertain part of the job by hand at first, so you validate the whole loop before building the expensive automation underneath it.

learningObjectives.text: Identify when a manual process behind the scenes is a legitimate v1 strategy
Recognize when 'fake it manually' would actually mislead your validation instead of helping it

contentSections.title: You don't have to build the hard part yet

contentSections.body: The invoice tracker's overdue calculation is simple: a date comparison. But a different candidate idea — one that reads a contract PDF and flags unusual clauses — has a genuinely hard part: understanding contract language well enough to flag something as unusual. Building that properly could take months on its own.

contentSections.scenario:
You want to test the contract-flagging idea without spending months on the hard part.

**Version A:** Build the full pipeline — PDF parsing, clause extraction, a trained classifier for "unusual" — before showing it to anyone.

**Version B:** Build a simple form where someone uploads a contract, you personally read it and flag anything unusual by hand, and email them the results within a day — while telling them plainly that a human is doing the reading for now.
contentSections.question: Which version actually tests whether this idea is worth building?

options.label: Version A
Version B
Neither — this needs the real pipeline to mean anything

feedback.a: Version A spends months building the hardest, most uncertain part before finding out whether anyone actually wants the finished experience — if the answer turns out to be no, or if what counts as "unusual" turns out to be different from what you assumed, those months are gone.
feedback.b: Right. Version B tests the actual thing that matters — does someone want this service, delivered this way, at this speed — using you as the hard part instead of a system you haven't built. If it turns out nobody wants it, or what people actually mean by "unusual" surprises you, you find out in days, not months, and you found out from real usage, not a guess.
feedback.neither: The whole point of faking the hard part is that the *experience* being tested — someone uploads a contract, gets flagged clauses back quickly — doesn't require the automation to be real yet. What needs to be real is the loop the user goes through, not the internals.

contentSections.concept: **When the hardest, most uncertain part of a job is also the part you're least sure people even want, do it by hand first.** You're testing the loop — the request, the delivery, the reaction — not proving you can automate something before you know it's worth automating.

contentSections.body: This only works with one condition attached: **be honest with the person that a human is doing it, at least until you've built the real thing.** "I'll personally review your contract and email you back within a day" is a legitimate, if unscalable, product. Quietly pretending a human-run process is an automated one is a different thing — a version of the earlier lesson's "be honest about what a tool costs and what happens when it's not available," applied to your own service instead of a vendor's.
Fake the hard, uncertain part by hand first — but tell the person a human is doing it. You're testing whether the loop is wanted, not proving you can automate it yet.

contentSections.title: When faking it would mislead you

contentSections.body: For the invoice tracker, faking the overdue calculation by hand would be pointless — it's a date comparison, not a hard or uncertain judgment call. Doing it manually wouldn't test anything real; it would just be slower than building the two-line function.

contentSections.question: You're scoping a tool that suggests a fair split of shared vacation-rental costs among a group. The math (splitting a total by nights stayed) is simple. Should you fake this part by hand, or just build it?
contentSections.answer: Just build it. This isn't the hard, uncertain part of the idea — it's a straightforward calculation, similar to the invoice tracker's overdue check. Faking it manually would only slow you down without testing anything you're actually unsure about.
contentSections.hint: Ask the same two questions from the lesson: is this genuinely hard to build, and are you actually uncertain whether people want it?

contentSections.body: The manual-behind-the-curtain move only makes sense when two things are both true: the automated version would be genuinely hard or slow to build, *and* you're still uncertain whether the finished experience is even wanted. If the hard part is easy to build (a date comparison), fake-it-by-hand just adds friction for nothing. If the experience is already fully validated and the only question left is engineering, you're past the point where faking it helps — at that point you're just delaying real work.
Fake the hard part only when it's both genuinely hard to build and genuinely uncertain whether it's wanted. Otherwise, just build it — it's the easy part for a reason.

title: Scoping to a week you might spend in bed
description: Building a real buffer into a one-week scope for the version of the week that doesn't go as planned, without inflating the scope back up to cover it.

learningObjectives.text: Build a genuine time buffer into a scope without expanding what the v1 does
Identify which stage of a scoped build to protect first when a bad day happens

contentSections.title: A week that assumes seven good days is a lie

contentSections.body: You scope the invoice tracker to exactly seven days of steady, even effort. On day four, you're flat on your back with a migraine and get nothing done. The scope, built on an assumption of seven equal days, doesn't survive contact with one bad one.

A one-week scope that only works if every day goes well isn't actually a one-week scope — it's a best-case estimate wearing a deadline's clothes. The fix isn't to give the whole project more time by default, which just lets everything expand back to the size lesson one warned about. It's to build the buffer into the plan itself: **scope the three required features (from lesson three) to fit in four or five good days, not seven, and treat the rest as slack that absorbs a bad one.**

This matters more here than in most curricula, because a scope that assumes uniform energy every day is a scope that keeps failing for exactly the same reason, over and over, for anyone whose capacity varies. Building the buffer in isn't a lesser version of scoping — it's what makes a one-week scope actually survivable.

contentSections.problem: You have three required features for the invoice tracker (CSV import, overdue calculation, results list) and a nominal one-week deadline. Build a schedule that survives one bad day.

steps.label: Count real working days, not calendar days
steps.work: Seven calendar days, but budget for five actual working sessions — assume two days (not necessarily consecutive) will be unavailable or low-capacity.
steps.why: Planning against five sessions instead of seven is what actually creates the buffer, rather than hoping nothing goes wrong.

steps.label: Order the required features by risk, not by preference
steps.work: CSV import first (most likely to have surprising real-world formatting issues), overdue calculation second (well-understood, low risk), results list third (mostly straightforward display work).
steps.why: Front-loading the riskiest, most unpredictable piece means a bad day is more likely to cost you time on the low-risk parts, which are easier to compress or finish quickly when you do have a good session.

steps.label: Name the one thing that ships even in the worst case
steps.work: If only three good sessions happen instead of five, the CSV import and overdue calculation, shown as a plain list with no formatting, is still a genuinely useful, shippable thing.
steps.why: This is the actual bad-day path for the build itself — a version that's smaller than your target v1 but still does the one validated job.

steps.label: Decide what gets cut first if the buffer runs out
steps.work: The results-list formatting is the first thing to simplify further — plain text instead of a styled table — because it doesn't touch the one job's correctness, only its presentation.
steps.why: Knowing this in advance means a bad week doesn't turn into a scramble to figure out what to cut under pressure — the decision was already made calmly.

faded.problem: Now do the same for a different scoped idea: a tool with two required features — matching two people's calendars to suggest a shared free hour, and displaying the result as a simple list of options.

blanks.prompt: How many real working sessions would you budget against, out of seven calendar days?
blanks.why: The same buffer principle applies regardless of the specific features — plan against fewer sessions than calendar days allow.

blanks.prompt: Which of the two features should come first, and why (in a few words)?
blanks.answer: the calendar-matching logic, because it's the riskier, less predictable part
blanks.why: The display of results is comparatively simple and predictable; front-loading the uncertain part protects the schedule the same way it did for the invoice tracker.

blanks.prompt: What's the smallest version that still ships if only three sessions happen?
blanks.answer: the calendar matching working correctly, shown as a plain unformatted list of shared time slots
accept: matching works, shown as a plain list
blanks.why: This names, in advance, the true floor of the build — a version smaller than the target but still doing the one validated job.

contentSections.procedure: **Budget fewer working sessions than calendar days. Front-load the riskiest required feature. Name, in advance, the smallest version that still ships. Decide what simplifies first, before you're under pressure to decide.**

contentSections.body: Budget for five good sessions in a seven-day week, not seven — and decide in advance what ships if only three happen.

contentSections.title: The floor is still a real product

contentSections.body: Three good sessions happened instead of five. What ships is CSV import plus overdue calculation, shown as a plain list with no styling at all. It's less than you hoped for on day one. It's also exactly the one job, done completely, that five people told you they needed.

contentSections.question: The floor version — import plus calculation, completely unstyled — is now live. Roughly how much effort would adding basic styling back take, compared to what it took to build the required list in the first place?
contentSections.answer: Usually a small fraction of the original effort. That's exactly why it was safe to defer in lesson one and three — presentation polish is cheap to add back once there's slack again, and it was never load-bearing for the one job to begin with.
contentSections.hint: Compare the size of "make it look nicer" to the size of "make the core calculation correct in the first place."

contentSections.body: The floor version from the worked example isn't a failure state — it's the same "one job, done completely" standard from lesson two, just without the presentation polish that was never part of the required list anyway. This is worth sitting with: a bad week doesn't have to mean shipping something broken or half-done, if the scope was built correctly from the start. It means shipping the honest floor of a well-scoped plan, which is still a real, useful thing.
A well-scoped v1's floor is still the one job, done completely — just without polish that was never required in the first place.

title: Cut seven bloated specs to a week's work
description: Seven drills applying the cut test, the one-job standard, and the buffer-planning method to specs you haven't seen before.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the cut test and one-job standard to unfamiliar feature lists
Recognize scope creep and buffer failures in realistic build scenarios

contentSections.body: Seven drills across this module's skills, from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Nothing here is timed.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Scope your tool to a one-week build
description: Take your validated idea and produce a real, honest one-week scope: the one job, the required list, the cut list, and the floor that ships on a bad week.

learningObjectives.text: Produce a scoped spec with a precise one-job statement and a short required list
Define an explicit cut list and a bad-week floor version

contentSections.body: You have a validated idea from module two. This lab turns it into a real, written scope — the kind you could hand to yourself on day one of the build and not have to think about scope again until it's done.

contentSections.title: Your scoped spec
contentSections.brief: Use the idea you validated in the previous module's lab. If it was killed, use the strongest surviving candidate from your idea log instead. The deliverable is a real, specific scope — not a wish list.
contentSections.deliverable: A scoped spec with a precise one-job statement, an explicit required list, an explicit cut (deferred) list, and a named floor version that would still ship on a bad week.

stages.title: Write the one-job statement
stages.instructions: Write one precise sentence naming the single job your v1 has to do completely, drawn from what actually showed up across most of your validation conversations — not a fresh guess. Test it: could a stranger read this sentence and know exactly what the tool does and doesn't do yet?
stages.checkpoint: You have one sentence, and it's precise enough that two different people reading it would picture the same tool.

stages.title: Run the cut test on a full feature list
stages.instructions: List every feature you can think of for this idea — aim for at least eight to ten, even ones you suspect won't survive. For each, ask: does the one job still work without it? Sort into required and deferred. If required has more than three items, go back and narrow the one-job statement.
stages.checkpoint: You have a required list of three items or fewer, and a deferred list with everything else, each item legibly sorted with a one-line reason.

stages.title: Decide where to fake the hard part, if anywhere
stages.instructions: Look at your required list. Is any part of it both genuinely hard to build and something you're still uncertain people want? If so, describe how you'd do that part manually for the first users instead of building it, and how you'd tell them a human is doing it. If nothing on your required list fits both conditions, write one sentence saying so and why.
stages.checkpoint: You've either named a specific manual-behind-the-curtain plan, or explicitly concluded none is needed and said why.

stages.title: Build the buffer and name the floor
stages.instructions: Budget your required list against five working sessions, not seven calendar days. Order the required items by risk, riskiest first. Name, in one or two sentences, the smallest version that would still ship if only three sessions happened — and confirm it still does the one job, even without polish.
stages.checkpoint: You have a session-ordered plan and a named floor version that's still the one job, done completely, just without extras.

rubric.criterion: The one-job statement is precise and validation-backed
rubric.meets: One sentence, specific enough that two readers would picture the same tool, drawn from what most validation conversations actually surfaced.

rubric.criterion: The required list has three items or fewer
rubric.meets: Each required item breaks the one job if removed; if the list is longer, the one-job statement gets renarrowed until it's short.

rubric.criterion: The deferred list is explicit, not implied
rubric.meets: Every cut feature is named on the list, not just silently dropped — deferred, not forgotten.

rubric.criterion: The manual-behind-the-curtain decision is deliberate
rubric.meets: Either a specific plan for faking a hard, uncertain part by hand with honest disclosure, or an explicit reasoned conclusion that none is needed.

rubric.criterion: A real bad-week floor is named
rubric.meets: The floor version is smaller than the target but still completes the one job — not a broken or half-working state.

rubric.criterion: It reads as a real plan, not a wish list
rubric.meets: Someone could start building from this document tomorrow morning without asking you a single clarifying question.

contentSections.body: A scope with a precise one job, a short required list, an explicit cut list, and a named bad-week floor is a plan you can actually build from — not just a smaller wish list.

title: Checkpoint — Cutting It Down to Shippable
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from the previous one, two from further back. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's and earlier modules' core distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Checkpoint — Cutting It Down to Shippable

questions.from: This module — Cutting It Down to Shippable
questions.prompt: What's the difference between "smallest possible" and "smallest useful"?

options.label: Smallest possible shrinks a big idea's features; smallest useful does one complete job with what people already have
They're the same thing, just worded differently
Smallest useful always means fewer total hours of work

questions.explanation: A miniature clone of a big tool (fewer features of everything) rarely fits a week. A tool that does one job completely, using data people already have, does.

questions.from: This module — Cutting It Down to Shippable
questions.prompt: Why are four features at 70% worth less than one feature at 100%, at equal total effort?

options.label: A user can't rely on something that mostly works — mostly working is functionally not working
70% features always have more bugs
Users always prefer fewer features

questions.explanation: Reliability, not effort or bug count, is what makes a feature useful. Zero fully-reliable features means nothing a user can actually depend on, regardless of how much work went in.

questions.from: This module — Cutting It Down to Shippable
questions.prompt: How do you decide which items on a feature list are required for v1?

options.label: Ask whether the one job still works without it — if yes, defer it; if no, it's required
Keep whichever features are easiest to build
Keep whichever features you personally find most exciting

questions.explanation: The cut test runs entirely off whether the precisely-defined one job still functions without the feature — not ease of building or personal excitement, both of which are unrelated to whether the job actually needs it.

questions.from: This module — Cutting It Down to Shippable
questions.prompt: When is faking the hard part by hand a legitimate v1 strategy?

options.label: When the part is both genuinely hard to build and you're still uncertain whether the finished experience is wanted — and you tell the user a human is doing it
Whenever a feature would take more than a day to build
Only for features nobody has validated yet

questions.explanation: Both conditions have to hold — hard to build AND uncertain whether it's wanted — and disclosure to the user is required. Faking an easy, well-understood part just adds friction for nothing.

questions.from: This module — Cutting It Down to Shippable
questions.prompt: Why budget five working sessions instead of seven calendar days for a one-week scope?

options.label: It builds in a real buffer for a bad day, without inflating what the v1 has to do
It's a superstition with no real effect on outcomes
It means the required list should be made longer to compensate

questions.explanation: The buffer is what lets a real bad day happen without blowing the deadline or forcing a scramble — and it works specifically by NOT expanding the required list to fill the extra nominal time.

questions.from: This module — Cutting It Down to Shippable
questions.prompt: A friend suggests a reasonable, small-sounding addition two days into a scoped build. What's the recommended response?

options.label: Log it as deferred and keep building the required list — "not now" is different from "never"
Add it immediately since it sounds small
Tell them it will never be supported

questions.explanation: "Small" additions rarely stay small once you're inside them, and rejecting the idea outright throws away real signal for no benefit. Deferring it — writing it down, not building it now — protects the schedule without closing the door.

questions.from: This module — Cutting It Down to Shippable
questions.prompt: What should the bad-week floor version of a well-scoped tool still do?

options.label: The one validated job, completely, just without presentation polish
As many features as possible, even if none work fully
Nothing — a bad week means nothing ships

questions.explanation: A well-built buffer means the floor is still a complete version of the one job, minus polish that was never on the required list in the first place — not a broken or empty result.

questions.from: This module — Cutting It Down to Shippable
questions.prompt: What's the sanity check if a cut test's required list comes out to seven or eight items?

options.label: The one-job statement was probably defined too broadly — go back and narrow it
Just build all seven or eight — the test found real requirements
Cut randomly until the list is short enough

questions.explanation: A long required list is a signal about the job definition, not a signal that the idea genuinely needs that much load-bearing machinery — the fix is re-narrowing the one job, not building through the long list or cutting arbitrarily.

questions.from: The previous module — Finding Out Before You Build
questions.prompt: Why do stated future intentions produce inflated yes rates?

options.label: A hypothetical yes doesn't have to compete with real switching costs and existing habits
Survey respondents are usually paid to answer positively
The questions are typically worded confusingly

questions.explanation: Nothing in the moment of answering a hypothetical forces the responder to weigh it against real habits or costs — the same reason this module insists on precise, validation-backed scope decisions instead of guesses.
