questions.prompt: What's the tell that an annoyance is idiosyncratic rather than shared?

options.label: The fix depends on a system, naming convention, or setup only you built or use
It's something you feel strongly about
You haven't mentioned it to anyone yet

questions.explanation: Whether the cause survives being swapped onto a different person with a normal setup is the test — the same instinct this module uses when checking whether a required feature is load-bearing or just something you personally got attached to.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: "Everyone" means nobody chose it
description: Why an audience defined as 'everyone' isn't ambitious, it's undecided — and how that shows up as a stalled tool with no way to break design ties.

learningObjectives.text: Recognize 'everyone' as an unmade decision rather than a large market
Explain how a vague audience produces unresolvable design disagreements

contentSections.title: The audience that isn't a decision

contentSections.body: You ask a founder who her expense-tracking tool is for. "Honestly, anyone who has expenses — freelancers, small businesses, even individuals budgeting." Eighteen months later, the tool has a little bit for each of those, and none of them love it.

contentSections.scenario:
Two answers to "who is this for?"

**Answer A:** "Anyone who needs to track expenses."

**Answer B:** "Solo freelance photographers who bill clients for travel and gear rentals, and currently track it in a phone notes app because it's faster than opening a spreadsheet mid-shoot."
contentSections.question: Which answer is actually a decision you could design around?

options.label: Answer A
Answer B
Both — they describe the same underlying group, just at different zoom levels

feedback.a: "Anyone who needs to track expenses" describes almost every working adult. It doesn't tell you what device they're on, how much time they have, what they're already doing instead, or what would make them switch — so it can't actually settle any design question.
feedback.b: Right. This one tells you the device (phone, mid-task), the current workaround (a notes app), the specific cost type (travel and gear rentals), and why speed beats structure for this person. Every one of those facts can settle a real design argument later.
feedback.both: They're not the same zoom level with different words — Answer A contains millions of people with contradictory needs (a freelancer mid-shoot and a household budgeter reviewing expenses once a month need different things), while Answer B picks one specific situation precisely enough to design for.

contentSections.concept: **"Everyone" isn't a big, ambitious audience — it's an audience decision you haven't made yet.** A useful audience definition is specific enough that two different people reading it would picture the same person in the same situation.

contentSections.body:
The appeal of "everyone" is obvious: naming a narrow audience feels like giving something up, and nobody wants to turn away potential users before they've even built anything. But "everyone" doesn't actually protect optionality — it just delays a decision that gets made anyway, later, usually by whichever loud user or investor spoke most recently, instead of by you, deliberately, with your validation notes in front of you.

This connects directly to the scoping work from the last module: you can't run the cut test ("does the one job still work without this feature?") without knowing whose job it is. "Everyone's" job includes contradictory jobs — a freelancer wants speed, a small business owner wants approval workflows, an individual budgeter wants monthly summaries. Trying to serve all three at once is exactly how three required features became eleven.
"Everyone" isn't an ambitious audience — it's a decision you're avoiding, and it gets made for you later, badly.

contentSections.title: What a vague audience actually costs you

contentSections.body: Two teammates disagree about whether the expense tracker should default to detailed itemized entries or one quick lump-sum entry. They argue for forty minutes. Neither can win, because neither of them can say who's right for — there's no specific person to check the answer against.

contentSections.scenario: You're watching a team argue about product decisions for a tool with a vague, "everyone" audience.
contentSections.question: Which of these disagreements is a symptom of the vague-audience problem specifically? Select all that apply.

items.label: Whether entries should be detailed and itemized, or one quick lump sum
Which database engine to use for storing entries
Whether to build the mobile app or the desktop app first
What shade of blue to use for the primary button
Whether onboarding should be a thirty-second quick-start or a guided five-minute setup

explanation.detail-vs-speed: This is a direct symptom — a specific freelancer mid-shoot wants speed; a small business owner reviewing books monthly might want detail. Without knowing which person you're building for, this argument has no way to resolve.
explanation.database-choice: This is a technical decision that mostly doesn't depend on who the user is — it depends on data volume and query patterns, which a vague audience doesn't really block you from reasoning about.
explanation.mobile-vs-desktop: This depends entirely on where the specific person actually is when the problem happens — mid-task on a phone, or reviewing books at a desk. A vague audience leaves this genuinely unanswerable.
explanation.color-choice: A cosmetic choice, mostly independent of audience specificity — this would stall for reasons unrelated to who the user is.
explanation.onboarding-length: This depends on how much attention and context the specific user has in the moment they first open the tool — exactly the kind of thing a real, specific person's situation would settle and 'everyone' can't.

contentSections.synthesis: The tell for a vague-audience argument is that it's unresolvable by more discussion — it needs a specific person's actual situation to check the answer against, not a better argument.

contentSections.body: An argument that four rounds of discussion can't resolve is often a symptom of a vague audience, not a hard design problem.

title: Describing a real person's situation
description: Writing a user description specific enough to actually settle design arguments, grounded in your own validation notes rather than an invented persona.

learningObjectives.text: Write a user description specific enough to resolve real design decisions
Ground a user description in real validation evidence rather than invention

contentSections.body: A marketing team's persona document describes "Sarah, 32, ambitious marketing manager who loves efficiency and hates wasted time." It has a stock photo attached. It has never once settled a single product argument, because nothing in it is specific enough to check anything against.

contentSections.scenario:
Two user descriptions for the invoice tracker from earlier modules.

**Description A:** "Maya, a busy, detail-oriented freelancer who values her time and wants tools that just work."

**Description B:** "A solo freelance designer with 3-5 active clients, who currently checks for overdue invoices by scrolling back through email once a week on Sunday night, and has, more than once, missed one for two weeks."
contentSections.question: Why does Description B actually work as a design tool and Description A doesn't?

options.label: B is longer, so it contains more information
B names a specific current behavior, frequency, and a real failure, which are checkable facts a decision can be tested against
B has a more realistic-sounding name

feedback.length: Length isn't really the mechanism — you could write three vague sentences instead of one and it still wouldn't help. What matters is what kind of information is in there.
feedback.specificity: Right. "Checks once a week, on Sunday night, by scrolling email" and "missed one for two weeks" are checkable, specific facts — you can ask "would a Sunday-night weekly digest fit this?" and get a real answer. "Values her time" can't be checked against anything.
feedback.name: The name is irrelevant — swapping "Maya" for anything else changes nothing about whether the description helps you design.

contentSections.mechanism: **A user description is only useful if it contains checkable facts: what they currently do, how often, on what device, and what's gone wrong because of it.** Adjectives like "busy" or "detail-oriented" describe a feeling about the person, not a fact you can design against.

contentSections.body: The reliable source for this description is your own validation notes from module two, not invention — the person who told you, in their own words, exactly how they currently handle the problem is a far better source than a persona built from imagination. If your validation notes are thin on specifics, that's itself useful information: it means you need one or two more real conversations before you can write a description this module actually needs, not that you should fill the gap with a plausible-sounding guess.
A user description only helps if it's built from checkable facts — current behavior, frequency, device, a real failure — not adjectives about how the person feels.

contentSections.title: Writing it from your own notes

contentSections.body: You reread your validation conversations for the invoice tracker. Three of five people specifically mentioned checking for overdue invoices on their phone, in a spare moment, not sitting at a desk with the spreadsheet open. That detail alone should already be shaping a decision.

contentSections.intro: Build a real user description for the invoice tracker from these three real validation quotes: "I check on my phone between client calls, honestly"; "I forget until a client asks where their invoice is"; "I've got maybe four active clients at once, I could probably do it from memory if I tried but I don't trust myself to."

fields.prompt: What device and moment should the description name?
options: Checking on their phone, in spare moments between other tasks
Sitting at a desktop with the spreadsheet already open
Whatever device happens to be nearby
fields.correctValue: Checking on their phone, in spare moments between other tasks
fields.feedback: This is what the quote directly says — naming it precisely tells you the tool needs to work well on a phone, in a quick glance, not as a desktop-first dashboard.

fields.prompt: What should the description say triggers the check?
options: A client asks where their invoice is — a reactive, slightly embarrassing moment
A calendar reminder they set themselves
A scheduled weekly review habit
fields.correctValue: A client asks where their invoice is — a reactive, slightly embarrassing moment
fields.feedback: The quote says "I forget until a client asks" — that's a specific, slightly uncomfortable trigger, and it tells you the tool's real job might be proactive: catching this before the client has to ask, not just answering when asked.

fields.prompt: What should the description say about how many clients and how they cope today?
options: About four active clients, small enough to almost manage from memory but not quite trusted to
Dozens of clients, requiring serious organizational tooling
An unspecified number, to keep the description broad
fields.correctValue: About four active clients, small enough to almost manage from memory but not quite trusted to
fields.feedback: This is a real, checkable scale fact from the quote — it tells you the tool doesn't need to handle hundreds of clients elegantly; it needs to beat "almost trustable memory" for about four.

contentSections.synthesis: Put together: "A solo freelancer with about four active clients, who currently finds out an invoice is overdue when a client asks about it, and checks status on their phone in spare moments rather than at a desk." Every clause in that sentence came from a real quote, and every clause can now settle a design argument — phone-first, proactive-not-just-reactive, small-scale.

contentSections.body: Build the description clause by clause from real quotes — device, trigger, scale — not from an imagined persona with a stock photo.

title: Where those people already are
description: Finding the specific place a defined user already spends time — for distribution, for further validation, and for testing — instead of a generic 'social media' plan.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the specific places a defined user already spends time
Distinguish a real, identifiable community from a vague platform-level guess

contentSections.title: Specific enough to actually go there

contentSections.body: "I'll market it on social media" is a plan with no next Tuesday attached to it — there's no specific action that follows from it. "I'll post in r/freelanceDesigners and the two Discord servers I'm already in for illustrators" has an action attached to it by Thursday.

contentSections.question: Put these steps of finding where your defined user actually is in order.
steps: Reread your user description for specific clues — their profession, their current workaround, their tools
List the specific communities, forums, or groups tied to that profession or workaround, by name
Check whether you're already a legitimate member of any of them (per module one's posture on communities)
For any you're not in, decide whether joining honestly is realistic before you'd need to post anything
Prioritize the ones where you can post as an existing member over the ones where you'd be a stranger
contentSections.explanation: This mirrors module one's community-sourcing lesson directly — the user description tells you who to look for, naming specific real places by name is what makes the plan actionable, and prioritizing communities you're already legitimately part of avoids the cold-pitch problem from that same module.

contentSections.body:
"Freelance designers" as an audience could mean a dozen different platforms. "Solo freelance designers with 3-5 clients who currently track invoices via email" narrows it fast: professional Discord servers for freelance creatives, subreddits for specific freelance disciplines, invoicing-adjacent communities (accounting-for-freelancers groups, where people already discuss money workflows), and any existing tool's user community where people are actively complaining about the exact workaround you're replacing.

The specificity of the user description from lesson two is what makes this lesson possible at all — you can't name real communities for "everyone," but you can name three or four real, specific ones for "a solo freelance designer checking invoices on their phone."
"Social media" isn't a plan. A named, specific community your defined user actually belongs to is.

contentSections.title: The community you found versus the one you assumed

contentSections.body: You assume freelance photographers hang out on Instagram, because that's where their work is visible. When you actually ask two photographers where they go for business advice and tool recommendations, both say a specific private Facebook group you'd never have guessed.

contentSections.scenario:
You're deciding where your defined user — a solo freelance photographer — actually spends time discussing business tools and workflow problems.

**Guess:** Instagram, because that's where photographers showcase work.

**What two real photographers told you when asked directly:** a specific, named private Facebook group for wedding photographers, where they discuss pricing, client management, and tool recommendations daily.
contentSections.question: Which should you trust more?

options.label: The Instagram guess, since it's where the profession is visible online
What the two real photographers actually told you
Both — post in both places to be safe

feedback.guess: Visibility isn't the same as where business discussions happen — Instagram is where photographers show finished work to clients, which is a completely different context from where they go to discuss which invoicing tool to use.
feedback.told: Right. Where your work is publicly visible and where you go to discuss business tools with peers are often different places entirely — asking real people beats guessing from the outside every time.
feedback.both: Posting everywhere isn't free — it costs time and dilutes your presence in the place that actually matters. Once you have a real answer from real users, act on it rather than hedging against your own guess.

contentSections.concept: **Where a profession is visible and where that profession discusses tools and workflow problems are often two different places.** Ask your validated users directly where they'd have expected to find something like this, rather than guessing from what's publicly visible about their work.

contentSections.body: Ask your users directly where they go to discuss tools and workflow — don't infer it from where their finished work happens to be visible.

title: Designing for the person with no energy today
description: Building for the version of your defined user who's tired, distracted, or having a bad day — because that's a real and frequent state, not an edge case.

learningObjectives.text: Design a core interaction for a low-energy or low-attention state, not just an ideal one
Identify which of a tool's steps assume the user's best day, and simplify them

contentSections.title: The version of your user having a bad day

contentSections.body: The invoice tracker's onboarding assumes ten focused minutes: connect an account, set preferences, review a tutorial. Your actual defined user checks invoices in a spare moment between client calls. Ten focused minutes doesn't exist in that person's day, good day or bad.

contentSections.scenario: A habit-tracking app requires setting up categories, goals, and reminder times before it shows any value. Usage data shows most people who abandon it do so during that setup, not after using it.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism behind this drop-off?

options.label: The categories offered aren't good enough
The app assumes a user's best-attention state to even get started, and most real visits happen in a lower-energy, lower-attention moment
The reminder times are confusing

feedback.categories: Category quality wouldn't explain drop-off during setup specifically, before anyone's even seen a category — the problem is earlier than that.
feedback.energy: Right. A multi-step setup assumes someone has ten minutes of focused attention available right now, but for a huge share of real visits — someone opening the app in a spare thirty seconds — that assumption is simply false, regardless of how good the setup screens are.
feedback.reminders: This might be a real problem too, but it wouldn't explain people leaving *during setup*, before they've reached reminder configuration.

contentSections.mechanism: **A tool's core interaction is often designed for the user's best possible moment, but most real usage happens in an ordinary or worse one.** The fix isn't better instructions for the ten-minute setup — it's a version of the core value that doesn't require ten focused minutes at all.

contentSections.body: This connects directly to your own user description from lesson two: if it names a specific low-attention moment (a phone check between calls, a glance while lying down, a quick look before a meeting), that moment should be the one your v1's core interaction is designed for — not a fallback you'll get to later. The badDayPath idea from this course's own pacing model applies just as much to the tool you're building: what's the version of this interaction that still works when the person has thirty seconds and no spare attention, not the version that works when they have ten minutes and are fully focused?
Design the core interaction for your user's ordinary, low-attention moment — not their best possible one — because that's when most real usage actually happens.

contentSections.title: Simplifying the step that assumes too much

contentSections.body: The invoice tracker's v1, per module three's scope, imports a CSV. But "export a CSV from your invoicing tool, then upload it" is itself a multi-step task that assumes focus and a desktop. On the phone, in a spare moment, that's not realistic.

contentSections.question: Given the defined user checks on their phone in spare moments, what would a lower-effort alternative to "export and upload a CSV" look like for getting their invoice data in?
contentSections.answer: Something like forwarding an invoice confirmation email to a dedicated address, or pasting a quick list of amounts and due dates as plain text — either removes the desktop-and-focus requirement the CSV export implicitly assumes, even if it's less structured than a full import.
contentSections.hint: The goal isn't a perfect data model — it's removing the assumption that the person has ten minutes at a desktop to prepare a file.

contentSections.body: This doesn't override module three's scoping work — it sharpens it. "Accept a CSV" was the right call for keeping v1 small, but it's worth checking that decision specifically against the low-attention moment from your user description, not just against build effort. Sometimes the easiest-to-build option (CSV import) and the easiest-to-use-on-a-bad-day option (forward an email) are different, and it's worth knowing that before you commit, even if you end up building the harder one anyway for good reasons.
Check your v1's easiest-to-build path against your user's lowest-energy moment — they're not always the same path, and it's worth knowing when they diverge.

title: Saying who it isn't for
description: Writing an explicit exclusion is what actually protects a specific audience definition from slowly drifting back into 'everyone.'

learningObjectives.text: Write an explicit statement of who a tool is not for
Use an exclusion statement to resolve a specific feature request

contentSections.title: The sentence that protects the other sentence

contentSections.body: Three months after launch, a small business owner with a bookkeeper and twelve clients asks for approval workflows, multi-user access, and audit logs. Every request is reasonable on its own. Granting all of them would quietly turn the solo-freelancer tool back into "everyone's" tool.

contentSections.code:
Who it's for: Solo freelancers who bill a handful of clients
and want to know what's overdue without digging through email.

Who it's not for: People who don't need this.
contentSections.question: What's wrong with the "who it's not for" line?

options.label: It's not specific enough to resolve any actual future request
It's too harsh in tone
It shouldn't exist at all — only positive audience statements are useful

feedback.vague: Right. "People who don't need this" is circular — it doesn't name teams, agencies, multi-user needs, or anything specific enough that a real future request could be checked against it. It has the shape of an exclusion without doing an exclusion's job.
feedback.harsh: Tone isn't really the issue here — this line could be worded warmly and still fail, because the problem is that it names nothing concrete.
feedback.unnecessary: The lesson's whole point is that the exclusion is what protects the inclusion from drifting — without it, reasonable one-off requests slowly pull the audience back toward everyone.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A working exclusion has to be as specific as the inclusion it's protecting — it should name the group, and ideally the specific need (multi-user, approval workflows, team accounts) that would pull the scope wide again. "People who don't need this" fails because it restates the inclusion rather than adding new information; a real version names the specific thing being turned away, so the decision is already made before the pressure of a real, sympathetic person asking for it arrives.

contentSections.body:
A specific audience definition (lesson two) tells you what to build. It doesn't, by itself, stop you from slowly building for other people too, one reasonable request at a time — that's exactly how "everyone" gets rebuilt after you thought you'd avoided it. The missing piece is a second, equally specific sentence: **who this explicitly isn't for, yet.**

For the invoice tracker: *"This is not for teams, agencies, or anyone who needs multiple people to see or edit the same invoices — if you need shared access or approval steps, this isn't the right tool yet."* That sentence does real work: the next time a reasonable multi-user request comes in, there's already a written answer, made calmly in advance, instead of a fresh, pressured decision made in the moment a specific person is asking.
A vague exclusion ("people who don't need this") does no work. A specific one names exactly what's being turned away, and why.

contentSections.title: Using it when the pressure is real

contentSections.body: The small business owner with twelve clients is a real person, asking politely, offering to pay more for the extra features. Saying no to a real paying customer feels different than writing an abstract policy in a quiet moment.

contentSections.question: The small business owner offers to pay double for shared, multi-user access — directly against your written exclusion. Does having written that exclusion in advance mean the answer has to be a permanent no?
contentSections.answer: No — it means the decision gets checked against something you already decided calmly, instead of being made fresh under pressure. It might still become a real, deliberately-scoped v2 for a newly and specifically defined audience later. "Not yet" and "never" are different answers, and the exclusion protects you from caving in the moment, not from ever changing your mind on purpose.
contentSections.hint: Think about what the exclusion actually protects against — a bad decision made under pressure, not necessarily all future expansion.

contentSections.body:
This is exactly why the exclusion has to be written in advance, calmly, before a specific sympathetic person is asking — the same discipline as module three's scope-creep case-sim. In the moment, with a real offer of money on the table, saying no feels like leaving value behind. Reading back your own exclusion statement, written when you weren't under that pressure, turns the decision back into something you already made rather than something you have to relitigate every time a reasonable person asks.

Saying no here isn't permanent, exactly like a deferred feature isn't permanently cut. It might become a genuine v2 for a different, more specific audience — "small agencies with 2-5 team members" is itself a real, specific audience someone could design for deliberately. It's just not this v1's audience, and the written exclusion is what makes that possible to say clearly instead of caving one request at a time.
The exclusion is written before the pressure arrives specifically so the decision doesn't have to be remade, under pressure, every single time.

title: Sharpen seven vague audience definitions
description: Seven drills applying this module's skills — turning vague audiences into checkable descriptions, finding where a user actually is, and writing exclusions that hold under pressure.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the module's audience-sharpening skills to unfamiliar scenarios
Recognize vague audience definitions and their symptoms

contentSections.body: Seven drills across this module's skills, from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Nothing here is timed.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Write the user definition for your tool
description: Produce a real, specific user definition for your scoped idea, grounded in real validation notes, that could actually settle a design disagreement.

learningObjectives.text: Write a checkable, evidence-grounded user description
Write an exclusion statement and test both against real design questions

contentSections.body: You have a scoped idea from module three and real validation notes from module two. This lab turns those into a user definition specific enough to actually settle arguments — not a persona document nobody ever opens again.

contentSections.title: Your user definition
contentSections.brief: Use your scoped idea and validation notes. If your idea was killed, use your strongest surviving candidate and the notes you have on it — the exercise is the same either way.
contentSections.deliverable: A user definition specific enough to settle three real design arguments, including an explicit exclusion statement.

stages.title: Write the description from real quotes
stages.instructions: Using your actual validation notes, write a user description with the checkable facts from lesson two: current behavior, device, frequency, and a real failure or cost, in the person's own words where you have them. If your notes are too thin to do this honestly, note specifically what's missing rather than inventing detail.
stages.checkpoint: Every clause in your description traces back to something a real person actually said or did, not an invented trait.

stages.title: Name where they actually are
stages.instructions: Name at least two specific, real communities or places your defined user spends time — not a platform in general. If you don't know yet, write the specific question you'd ask a real user to find out, per lesson three.
stages.checkpoint: You have named specific communities, or specific questions you'd ask to find them — not a generic platform guess.

stages.title: Design the low-energy version of the core moment
stages.instructions: Identify the lowest-attention, lowest-energy moment your user description implies (per lesson four), and write what the core interaction looks like in that moment specifically — not the ideal, fully-focused version.
stages.checkpoint: You have a described interaction built for the user's ordinary or worse moment, not their best one.

stages.title: Write the exclusion and test all three against real arguments
stages.instructions: Write a specific "who this isn't for, yet" sentence, naming a real group and the specific need that would pull scope wide again. Then write three real design questions this idea could plausibly face, and show, for each, how your description or exclusion settles it.
stages.checkpoint: You have a specific exclusion and three real design questions each resolved by a specific clause in your definition or exclusion — not a general appeal to "knowing your user."

rubric.criterion: The description is built from checkable facts
rubric.meets: Every clause traces to real behavior, device, frequency, or cost from actual validation notes, not invented adjectives.

rubric.criterion: The description is grounded in real evidence, not persona invention
rubric.meets: You can point to the specific quote or observation behind each claim, or you've flagged where evidence is missing.

rubric.criterion: Named communities are specific and real
rubric.meets: At least two named places, or specific questions to find them — never a bare platform name with no further detail.

rubric.criterion: The low-energy design decision is concrete
rubric.meets: A specific description of how the core interaction changes for the user's ordinary or bad moment, not a restatement of the ideal version.

rubric.criterion: The exclusion names a real group and a real reason
rubric.meets: The 'who it's not for' statement is as specific as the inclusion, naming a group and the specific need being deferred.

rubric.criterion: All three test questions are actually resolved
rubric.meets: Each of the three design questions is settled by pointing at a specific clause, not by restating that you 'know your user well.'

contentSections.body: A user definition earns its keep the moment it actually settles an argument you couldn't have settled without it.

title: Checkpoint — Who It's For
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from the previous one, two from further back. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's and earlier modules' core distinctions without looking them up

questions.from: This module — Who It's For
questions.prompt: Why is "everyone" a weak audience definition?

options.label: It's an unmade decision that gets made later, by whoever's loudest, instead of deliberately by you
It's technically inaccurate since no product truly serves everyone
It sounds unambitious to investors

questions.explanation: "Everyone" doesn't protect optionality — it defers a real decision to later, where it usually gets made badly, by whichever request or voice is loudest at the time, instead of deliberately from validation evidence.

questions.from: This module — Who It's For
questions.prompt: What makes a user description actually useful for design decisions?

options.label: Checkable facts — current behavior, device, frequency, a real failure — not adjectives about how the person feels
A realistic-sounding name and a stock photo
Being as long and detailed as possible

questions.explanation: "Busy and detail-oriented" can't be checked against anything. "Checks on their phone once a week, has missed one for two weeks" can be tested against a real design question.

questions.from: This module — Who It's For
questions.prompt: Why might Instagram be the wrong place to find where freelance photographers discuss business tools, even though it's where their work is visible?

options.label: Where work is publicly visible and where a profession discusses tools/workflow are often different places
Instagram doesn't allow business discussion at all
Photographers don't use Instagram professionally

questions.explanation: Visibility of finished work and where peer business discussions happen are frequently separate contexts entirely — the lesson's photographers actually discussed tools in a private Facebook group, not on Instagram.

questions.from: This module — Who It's For
questions.prompt: Why design a tool's core interaction for the user's ordinary or low-energy moment rather than their best one?

options.label: Most real usage happens in an ordinary or worse moment, not the user's ideal, fully-focused state
It's always cheaper to build the simpler version
Users with more energy don't need good design

questions.explanation: The habit-tracker example drops off during setup because most real visits happen in a lower-attention moment than the ten-minute setup assumes — designing for the ordinary moment is designing for where most usage actually occurs.

questions.from: This module — Who It's For
questions.prompt: What makes an exclusion statement ("who it's not for") actually do useful work?

options.label: It's as specific as the inclusion, naming a real group and the specific need being deferred
It's worded firmly and confidently
It exists at all, regardless of specificity

questions.explanation: "People who don't need this" is circular and settles nothing. A working exclusion names the specific group and specific need (team accounts, approval workflows) being turned away, so a future request can be checked against it.

questions.from: This module — Who It's For
questions.prompt: Why write the exclusion in advance, before a real sympathetic customer asks for the excluded thing?

options.label: Because it's much harder to say no in the moment, under real pressure, than to have already decided calmly beforehand
Because customers prefer receiving a written policy
Because it's a legal requirement

questions.explanation: This mirrors the scope-creep case-sim from the previous module — a reasonable request from a real, sympathetic person is much harder to defer in the moment than a decision already made calmly, in advance, without that pressure.

questions.from: This module — Who It's For
questions.prompt: Two teammates argue for forty minutes over detailed vs. quick-entry design, and neither can win. What does this suggest?

options.label: The audience is probably too vague to check the answer against a real person's situation
One of them is simply wrong and needs to be convinced
The feature itself is poorly conceived

questions.explanation: An argument that more discussion can't resolve is often a symptom of a vague audience — the question needs a specific person's real situation to check the answer against, not a better argument.

questions.from: This module — Who It's For
questions.prompt: A description says "solo freelancer with about four clients, checks invoice status on their phone in spare moments, finds out an invoice is overdue when a client asks." Which design decision does this most directly settle?

options.label: Whether the core interaction should be phone-friendly and proactive rather than desktop-first and purely reactive
What color scheme to use
Which database to use

questions.explanation: Phone, spare moments, and a reactive trigger (a client asking) directly settle whether the tool should be phone-first and should proactively flag overdue invoices before a client has to ask — exactly the kind of decision a vague audience couldn't resolve.

questions.from: The previous module — Cutting It Down to Shippable
questions.prompt: How do you decide which items on a feature list are required for v1?

options.label: Ask whether the one job still works without it — if yes, defer it; if no, it's required
Keep whichever features are easiest to build
Keep whichever features you personally find most exciting

questions.explanation: The cut test runs off whether the precisely-defined one job still functions without the feature — the same instinct this module uses when checking whether a design decision is actually settled by the user definition.

questions.from: Finding Out Before You Build
questions.prompt: Why is "what do you think?" a weak validation question?

options.label: It invites an opinion about a hypothetical, which is cheap to be nice about
People always lie when asked directly
It's too short to get a useful answer

questions.explanation: The problem isn't dishonesty — a hypothetical opinion costs nothing, so politeness fills the gap. This module's user descriptions are built from the same kind of behavior-based evidence this earlier module taught you to collect.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: Looking properly before assuming nothing exists
description: A real, disciplined search for existing solutions — including the ones that don't show up on the first page of an obvious search — before treating an idea as a genuine gap.

learningObjectives.text: Run a search for existing solutions that goes past the first obvious page of results
Recognize the tempting but weak reasoning behind 'I searched and found nothing'

contentSections.title: The five-minute search that missed everything

contentSections.body: You search "invoice overdue tracker" for thirty seconds, see a few generic accounting suites, conclude "nothing simple exists for freelancers specifically," and start building. Two months later, a beta tester mentions the exact tool you were building, by name, that she's used for a year.

contentSections.scenario:
Two searches for the same idea — a simple habit tracker built specifically for people with chronic fatigue who can't commit to daily streaks.

**Search A:** "habit tracker app" — thirty seconds, top five generic results, all built around daily streaks.

**Search B:** "habit tracker chronic illness," "habit tracker no streaks," a specific chronic-illness subreddit's pinned app-recommendations thread, and a specific accessibility-focused app directory.
contentSections.question: Which search actually tells you whether this idea has a real gap?

options.label: Search A
Search B
Neither — you can't really know without building it

feedback.a: "Habit tracker app" is the generic category search, and it surfaces the generic, most-funded competitors — the ones least likely to specifically target a chronic-illness audience with no-streak design. Finding nothing relevant here tells you almost nothing about whether a specific gap exists.
feedback.b: Right. Searching with the specific audience and specific design constraint baked in, plus checking exactly where that audience already discusses tools (the subreddit, the directory), is what would actually surface a niche competitor a generic search misses entirely.
feedback.neither: You genuinely can find out a great deal before building — a disciplined search using the audience's own language and their own gathering places, per this lesson, gets you real evidence about what already exists.

contentSections.concept: **A generic category search surfaces generic, well-funded competitors and misses the niche ones — which are often exactly the competitors closest to your specific, narrow idea.** Search using your specific audience's language and their own gathering places, not the category's obvious keyword.

contentSections.body:
This connects directly to the audience work from the last module: if you've defined a specific user precisely, you already have the vocabulary a real search needs — their specific situation, the words they'd use, the communities they're in. A search for "expense tracker" misses what a search for "expense tracker freelance photographer gear rentals," plus a look in the specific communities from module four, would find.

The most common failure here isn't laziness exactly — it's stopping at the first page of an obvious, generic search and treating silence as evidence of a gap, when it's often just evidence that you searched the wrong, too-broad term.
A generic search finds generic competitors. Search with your specific audience's language and their gathering places to find the real, niche ones.

contentSections.title: Where a real search actually looks

contentSections.body: Beyond a search engine, three places consistently surface competitors a keyword search misses: the app stores' own search and "similar apps" sections, the specific communities your defined user is already in (per module four), and directly asking a couple of your validated users what they've already tried.

contentSections.scenario: You're doing a proper pre-build competitor search for a niche idea.
contentSections.question: Which of these are genuinely part of a thorough search? Select all that apply.

items.label: Searching directly within app stores, including their "similar to this" suggestions on adjacent tools
Asking two or three of your already-validated users directly: "what have you already tried for this?"
One broad category search on a general search engine
Searching within the specific communities your defined user is already in
Trusting your gut sense that nothing like this exists, since you haven't personally seen it

explanation.app-store: App stores' own search and adjacency features surface real, shipped competitors that a general web search sometimes buries under content marketing and blog posts.
explanation.ask-users: This is one of the strongest sources available — the people you've already validated with have often already tried something, and they'll tell you exactly why it didn't stick, which is free competitive research plus a differentiation angle.
explanation.generic-search: A single broad search is the thing this lesson specifically warns is insufficient on its own — it's a fine starting point, not a complete search.
explanation.community-search: This is exactly where a niche competitor, invisible to a generic search, is most likely to be recommended by name.
explanation.trust-hunch: Not having personally seen something is not evidence it doesn't exist — this is exactly the reasoning that led to the freelancer building a tool that already existed, unbeknownst to them.

contentSections.synthesis: A real search combines a broad search, app-store search, community search, and direct questions to validated users — not any single one of these alone, and never just a gut sense.

contentSections.body: A real competitor search combines app-store search, community search, and asking validated users directly — never just a gut feeling that nothing exists.

title: Why an existing tool isn't good enough, specifically
description: Naming the precise, specific gap an existing tool leaves — not a vague sense that it's 'clunky' or 'not quite right' — as the actual foundation for a differentiation claim.

learningObjectives.text: Convert a vague dissatisfaction with an existing tool into a specific, testable gap
Distinguish a real gap from a personal taste mismatch with an existing tool

contentSections.title: "It's just not quite right" isn't a finding

contentSections.body: You've found the existing invoice tool your defined user already uses sometimes. Asked why they don't rely on it fully, they say: "it's fine, just not quite right for me." That sentence, on its own, doesn't tell you what to build differently.

contentSections.scenario: A freelancer says an existing time-tracking app is "just not quite right" for her. Pressed further, she says: "I have to open the app, tap start, remember to tap stop — I usually forget the stop part and lose track of the actual time."
contentSections.question: What's the actual, specific gap here?

options.label: The app's design is unappealing to her
The manual start/stop interaction doesn't match how she actually works, and she reliably forgets to stop it — a specific, structural mismatch
She just doesn't like tracking time in general

feedback.design: Nothing in her follow-up mentions how it looks — the actual complaint is about a specific interaction (manual start/stop) and a specific, repeated failure (forgetting to stop), not aesthetics.
feedback.structural: Right. The follow-up question turned a vague "not quite right" into something specific and structural: a manual step she reliably forgets, causing a reliably lost measurement. That's a gap you could actually design against — something closer to automatic or passive tracking.
feedback.dislike: If she genuinely disliked time tracking in general, this wouldn't be a promising idea at all — but her actual complaint is about a specific mechanic failing her, not the underlying task.

contentSections.mechanism: **"Not quite right" is where the conversation starts, not where it ends.** One good follow-up question — "what specifically happens when you try to use it?" — usually turns a vague dissatisfaction into a structural, nameable gap: a step people forget, a format that doesn't match their workflow, a false assumption about their situation baked into the tool's design.

contentSections.body:
This matters because "the existing tools are clunky" is not a differentiation claim anyone can build against — it's a feeling. "The existing tools require a manual start/stop that people using them for spontaneous work reliably forget" is a specific, checkable claim, and it points directly at what a genuinely different version would need to do differently (automatic detection, a passive log, a very fast one-tap correction instead of prospective tracking).

The method is the same behavior-based questioning from the validation module: ask what specifically happens when they try to use the existing tool, not just whether they like it.
"Not quite right" is a starting point. One follow-up — what specifically happens when you try to use it — usually finds the real, structural gap.

A different person says the same existing time-tracker "just feels sterile, I don't love using it." Pressed further: it tracks accurately, never loses data, and does everything she needs — she just finds the visual design unpleasant.

contentSections.question: Compare this response to the structural-gap example. Is "feels sterile, don't love using it, but it works fine" the same kind of signal as "I forget to tap stop and lose the data"?
contentSections.answer: No — this is closer to a taste mismatch than a structural gap. The tool works, does the job, and loses nothing; the complaint is aesthetic. That's real, and design does matter, but it's a much weaker foundation for a differentiation claim than a specific functional failure, and it's worth naming that distinction honestly rather than dressing up a taste preference as a validated gap.
contentSections.hint: Ask whether the follow-up revealed a specific functional failure, or just a feeling about how it looks and feels to use.

contentSections.body: Both kinds of dissatisfaction are real, but they're not equally strong foundations for a build decision. A structural gap (a workflow mismatch, a step people reliably forget, a false assumption about the user's situation) predicts that a genuinely different design would actually get adopted. A taste mismatch predicts that a *nicer-looking version of the same thing* might get adopted — a much smaller, riskier bet, and one that's easy to convince yourself is bigger than it is, because "I'll just make it nicer" feels like an easier project to imagine finishing.
A structural gap and a taste mismatch are both real, but only the first is a strong foundation for building something genuinely different.

title: Free, open source, and competing with those
description: Taking free and open-source tools seriously as real competition, and understanding the specific reasons people still don't use a free, technically-capable option.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate a free or open-source alternative as genuine competition, not a non-factor
Identify the specific non-price reasons a free tool goes unused

contentSections.title: "But it's free" isn't the same as "but it's no competition"

contentSections.body: You're scoping a paid invoice tracker. "There's a free open-source one on GitHub that does basically this," a friend mentions. Your first instinct is to dismiss it — free tools don't compete with a real product, right? Almost nobody you've talked to has actually heard of it, let alone used it.

contentSections.question: Put these steps of properly evaluating a free or open-source alternative in order.
steps: Actually try installing and using the free tool yourself, not just reading its description
Note specifically where it's hard: setup steps, technical knowledge required, missing features, abandonment
Ask your validated users if they've heard of it or tried it, and what happened if so
Identify the specific, nameable friction that keeps it from being the obvious default choice despite being free
Decide whether your idea directly removes that specific friction, or just duplicates the free tool with a price tag attached
contentSections.explanation: Free and open-source tools fail to be adopted for specific, nameable reasons — a rough setup process, no ongoing maintenance, a UI that assumes technical comfort most people don't have, missing a feature nobody's contributed. Naming that friction precisely, rather than assuming "free" and "real competitor" are mutually exclusive, is what tells you whether your paid idea has a genuine reason to exist or is just a nicer wrapper around something people could already get for nothing.

contentSections.body: "It's free, so it's not real competition" is one of the most tempting things to believe and one of the least reliable — plenty of genuinely useful free and open-source tools sit mostly unused because of setup friction, not because free options don't count. The honest question isn't "is it free," it's "why hasn't it already won, given that it's free and does roughly this?" Sometimes the answer really is discoverability (nobody's heard of it, and marketing is a real, defensible value-add). Sometimes it's a real, structural gap the free version has, same as lesson two's method. Sometimes — and this is worth being honest about — the free tool is genuinely good enough, and the actual gap you found was smaller than you hoped.
"It's free" doesn't mean "it's not competition." Ask why it hasn't already won, and name the specific friction keeping it from being everyone's default.

You actually install the free invoice tracker. It requires setting up a database connection and editing a config file by hand. It hasn't had a real update in fourteen months. It's genuinely powerful, and genuinely something almost none of your validated users would ever get through the setup for.

contentSections.scenario:
Two possible reasons a free tool goes unused by your specific defined audience.

**Reason A:** Setup requires editing a config file and understanding a database connection string — a real technical barrier for a non-technical freelancer.

**Reason B:** The tool's landing page uses a slightly dated color scheme.
contentSections.question: Which reason represents a real opportunity for your idea?

options.label: Reason A
Reason B
Both equally

feedback.a: Right. A genuine technical setup barrier, for an audience you've specifically defined as non-technical, is a real, structural reason the free option isn't actually available to your users — even though it's free in dollar terms, it's expensive in a currency (technical setup effort) your specific audience doesn't have.
feedback.b: A dated color scheme is a minor cosmetic issue, unlikely on its own to be the reason a genuinely useful free tool goes unused — this is a much weaker foundation for a differentiation claim than a real usability barrier.
feedback.both: These aren't equivalent — a config-file setup barrier for a non-technical audience is a structural gap in the sense of lesson two, while a color scheme complaint is closer to the taste-mismatch category that lesson flagged as weak.

contentSections.concept: **"Free" only means "available to your audience" if your specific audience can actually get through what it takes to use it.** A technical setup barrier, for an audience you've defined as non-technical, is a real gap — the same structural-versus-taste distinction from the last lesson, applied to free and open-source alternatives specifically.

contentSections.body: A free tool's real barrier to your specific audience — not its price — is where a genuine opportunity might actually be.

title: Building it anyway for a good reason
description: Deciding to build in a crowded space when you've identified a real, specific, defensible reason existing options fall short for your defined user.

learningObjectives.text: Articulate a defensible reason to build despite existing competition
Connect a differentiation claim to the specific gap found in earlier lessons

contentSections.title: A real reason names a specific gap and a specific user

contentSections.body: You now know: three existing invoice tools exist, all requiring manual entry; one free tool exists, requiring technical setup your defined user doesn't have. That's not "there's no competition" — it's a specific map of exactly where the gap actually is.

contentSections.scenario:
Two justifications for building the invoice tracker anyway.

**Justification A:** "There's a real gap for solo freelancers who check status on their phone in spare moments — every existing paid tool assumes desktop data entry, and the one free option requires technical setup this specific audience doesn't have."

**Justification B:** "I think I can build something better than what's out there."
contentSections.question: Which is a defensible reason to build anyway?

options.label: Justification A
Justification B
Both — confidence in your own ability matters too

feedback.a: Right. This names a specific audience, a specific structural gap (desktop-only data entry versus a phone-first spare-moment reality), and a specific reason the free alternative doesn't close it (technical setup barrier). Someone else could check every claim in it.
feedback.b: "I think I can build something better" is unfalsifiable — it doesn't name what's better, for whom, or why the existing options fall short. It's the kind of reasoning that feels like conviction but doesn't survive being written down and checked, which is the actual test this lesson is asking for.
feedback.both: Confidence isn't nothing, but it's not evidence — Justification A already contains everything worth trusting in Justification B (the belief you can build something worthwhile) plus the specific, checkable reasoning that makes it more than a hunch.

contentSections.concept: **A defensible reason to build into existing competition names the specific audience, the specific gap, and why existing options — paid and free — don't close it for that specific audience.** "I can do better" isn't a reason; it's a feeling wearing a reason's clothes.

contentSections.body: This is where every earlier module's work actually pays off directly: the specific user definition (module four) tells you who the gap is for, the validation notes (module two) tell you the gap is real and costly, and this module's competitor research tells you specifically why existing options — including free ones — don't already close it. A defensible "build it anyway" isn't optimism; it's those three things, stated together, checkable by someone else.
A defensible reason to build names the specific audience, the specific gap, and why existing options — paid and free — don't already close it for them.

"Better than the competition" is not a sentence you could hand to a stranger and have them understand what to expect. A real differentiation statement is short, specific, and names the exact gap being closed.

contentSections.problem: Write a real differentiation statement for the invoice tracker, using what's been established: three paid competitors require desktop data entry; one free tool requires technical setup; your defined user checks status on their phone in spare moments and finds out an invoice is overdue reactively, when a client asks.

steps.label: Name the audience precisely
steps.work: Solo freelancers with a handful of active clients who check invoice status on their phone, not at a desk.
steps.why: This is the audience from module four — without it, the differentiation floats free of any specific person it's actually for.

steps.label: Name what existing paid options assume
steps.work: Every existing paid tool assumes desktop data entry as the primary way of interacting with it.
steps.why: This is the specific gap from earlier in this module — checkable, and directly contradicted by how the defined user actually behaves.

steps.label: Name what the free option requires that this audience doesn't have
steps.work: The one free, open-source option requires editing a config file and setting up a database connection.
steps.why: This closes the obvious objection ("just use the free one") with a specific, real reason it doesn't work for this specific audience.

steps.label: State the differentiation as a single sentence
steps.work: "A phone-first invoice tracker for solo freelancers who need to know what's overdue in a spare moment, not at a desk — with none of the setup the free alternative requires."
steps.why: This sentence is checkable clause by clause against everything gathered in this module — it isn't a vibe, it's a claim someone could verify or dispute.

faded.problem: Now write a differentiation statement for a different idea: a meal-suggestion tool. Existing apps assume you're planning a full week in advance; your defined user decides what to cook the same evening, using what's already in the fridge. A free spreadsheet template exists but requires manually re-entering your fridge contents every time.

blanks.prompt: Name the audience precisely (a few words).
blanks.answer: someone deciding what to cook the same evening, using what's already in the fridge
accept: same-day cooks using existing fridge contents
blanks.why: This is the specific behavior that distinguishes them from the week-planning audience existing apps assume.

blanks.prompt: Name what existing apps assume, in a few words.
blanks.answer: that the user is planning a full week of meals in advance
blanks.why: This is the structural gap — a mismatch between what the tools assume and what this specific user actually does.

blanks.prompt: Name the free alternative's specific barrier for this audience.
blanks.answer: requires manually re-entering fridge contents every time, which defeats the purpose of a same-evening decision
blanks.why: This closes the "just use the free spreadsheet" objection with something specific and real.

blanks.answer: something like: "a same-evening meal suggestion tool for people cooking with what's already in the fridge, without the weekly-planning assumption of other apps or the manual re-entry the free spreadsheet requires"
accept: a sentence naming same-day cooking, no weekly planning, no manual re-entry
blanks.why: A checkable, specific claim, built the same way as the invoice tracker's.

contentSections.procedure: **Name the audience precisely. Name what existing paid options assume that doesn't fit them. Name what the free option requires that they don't have. State it as one checkable sentence.**

contentSections.body: A real differentiation statement is one checkable sentence built from the audience, the paid gap, and the free tool's specific barrier — not a vibe about being "better."

title: Building it anyway for a bad reason
description: Recognizing the rationalizations that dress up 'I want to build this anyway' as a strategic decision, and what to do when that's honestly the situation.

learningObjectives.text: Recognize common rationalizations for building despite a lack of real differentiation
Decide honestly whether to build for personal reasons, separate from a market claim

contentSections.title: The rationalizations that sound like reasons

contentSections.body: You did the research from this module and found: existing paid tools already do desktop entry fine, your defined user is comfortable with that, and the free tool, while clunky to set up, works fine once configured. There isn't really a gap. You want to build it anyway.

contentSections.scenario: You're about to build despite the research not showing a real gap. Here's your internal reasoning.
contentSections.question: Which of these are rationalizations rather than real reasons? Select all that apply.

items.label: "Mine will just have nicer UX" — with no specific structural gap named, just a general sense it'll be nicer
"I want to build this specifically to learn a technology I've been wanting to practice, and I'm not expecting it to be a business"
"The market is so big there's room for another one" — without a specific audience segment existing options are failing
"I want a project to show in my portfolio, and I know going in this probably won't get real users"
"Everyone secretly hates the leading tool" — based on your own frustration, without checking whether your validated users actually feel the same

explanation.better-ux: "Nicer UX" without a named structural gap is exactly the taste-mismatch pattern from lesson two, dressed up as a market reason — it might be true, but it's a much weaker foundation than this module asks for.
explanation.learning: This is an honest, separate reason that doesn't pretend to be a market opportunity — it's a legitimate reason to build something, as long as you're not also telling yourself a false story about validated demand.
explanation.market-big: "Big market, room for another one" is a classic rationalization — it says nothing about whether existing options actually fail anyone specifically, which is what this module has been asking you to establish.
explanation.portfolio: Same as the learning case — an honest, self-aware reason, clearly labeled as not a market claim, which is exactly what separates it from a rationalization.
explanation.everyone-hates: Generalizing your own frustration to "everyone" without checking is the idiosyncratic-versus-shared mistake from module one, reappearing here in a new context.

contentSections.synthesis: The dividing line isn't whether you build for a personal reason — it's whether you're honest with yourself about which kind of reason it is, and whether you're telling yourself a false story about market demand to justify a decision you've already made for other reasons.

contentSections.body: Building something for practice, for a portfolio, or just because you want to is completely fine — this course has never claimed every hour has to lead to a paying business. What isn't fine, and what costs real time later, is dressing up "I want to build this" as "I found a real gap" when the research from this module actually said otherwise. The tell is usually a rationalization that would apply to almost any idea, in almost any market, regardless of what the actual research found — "the market's big enough," "mine will just be better," "everyone secretly hates the leader."
Building for a personal reason (learning, portfolio) is fine, as long as you're honest it's that — not a market claim the research didn't actually support.

contentSections.title: What to do with an honest "no real gap"

contentSections.body: You're honest with yourself: there's no real gap for the invoice tracker specifically. But three of your competitor-research conversations mentioned, unprompted, a completely different frustration — nobody's built a good way to split a project's expenses with a subcontractor. That sounds familiar, because it's the same lead from module two's killed idea.

contentSections.question: You've honestly concluded there's no real competitive gap for your current idea. What's the most useful next move, based on this module and the idea-log habit from module one?
contentSections.answer: Log the specific finding (no structural gap, existing options already close it well enough) and treat this the same way module two treated a validation kill — check whether anything mentioned in passing during your research is a new, worth-logging candidate, rather than forcing the current idea forward anyway.
contentSections.hint: This is the same instinct as killing a validated idea early — a clean 'no' here is a good, cheap result, not a failure to push through.

contentSections.body: This closes the loop the whole track has been building: an idea log entry (module one) becomes a validated candidate (module two), gets scoped (module three), gets a specific user (module four), and finally gets checked against what already exists (this module). Finding "no real gap" at this last stage isn't wasted work — it's the same honest, cheap-relative-to-building result as an early validation kill, and it very often hands you the next candidate on the way out, exactly the way this course has been modeling from the start.
An honest 'no real gap' at this stage is still a good, cheap result — and it often hands you the next candidate on the way out.

title: Assess seven ideas against what exists
description: Seven drills applying this module's skills — real searches, structural versus taste gaps, free-tool evaluation, and telling a defensible reason from a rationalization.

learningObjectives.text: Apply this module's competitive-research skills to unfamiliar scenarios
Distinguish defensible build-anyway reasons from rationalizations under time pressure

contentSections.body: Seven drills across this module's skills, from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Nothing here is timed.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Do the competitive research on your idea
description: Run a real, disciplined competitor search on your own idea, evaluate at least five existing options honestly, and write a differentiation statement — or an honest 'no real gap' finding.

learningObjectives.text: Run a thorough, multi-source competitor search
Produce an honest, specific differentiation claim or an honest kill finding

contentSections.body: This is the last piece before your idea is a real, checked candidate: an honest look at what already exists, using every source from this module, ending in either a real differentiation statement or an honest, useful "no."

contentSections.title: Your competitive assessment
contentSections.brief: Use your scoped idea and defined user from the previous two modules. This lab requires actually trying real competing tools, not just reading about them.
contentSections.deliverable: A written assessment of five existing tools (paid and free/open-source) and a specific differentiation statement, or an honest, evidence-based finding that no real gap exists.

stages.title: Search properly across all sources
stages.instructions: Search using your specific audience's language (module four), not just the generic category term. Check app stores, the specific communities your user is in, and ask at least two validated users directly what they've already tried. List every tool you find, including at least one free or open-source option.
stages.checkpoint: You have a list of at least five real tools, found through more than one of these methods — not just a single generic search.

stages.title: Actually try five of them
stages.instructions: For each of the five, actually use it (or its demo, trial, or documentation if a full trial isn't possible) — don't rely on marketing copy. For each, write down the specific friction: what's clunky, what it assumes about the user that's wrong for your specific audience, what it costs (dollars, setup time, technical requirement).
stages.checkpoint: You have five real, specific friction notes — not five vague impressions.

stages.title: Sort each gap: structural or taste
stages.instructions: For each of the five, decide whether the gap you found is structural (a workflow mismatch, a step people forget, a real barrier for your specific audience) or a taste mismatch, per lesson two. Be honest — don't inflate a taste complaint into a structural one to make your case look stronger.
stages.checkpoint: Each of the five tools is honestly sorted, with a one-line reason for the sorting.

stages.title: Write the differentiation, or the honest kill
stages.instructions: If at least one real structural gap survived the sort, write a one-sentence differentiation statement per lesson four's method: audience, what paid options assume, what the free option requires. If nothing structural survived, write an honest finding instead, and name anything mentioned in passing during your research that might be a new idea-log candidate.
stages.checkpoint: You have either a checkable one-sentence differentiation statement, or an honest kill finding plus any new lead worth logging.

rubric.criterion: The search used more than one method
rubric.meets: At least a specific-language search, an app-store or community search, and a direct question to validated users all appear in the record.

rubric.criterion: At least one free or open-source option was genuinely evaluated
rubric.meets: A free/open-source alternative was actually tried, not dismissed on the basis of being free.

rubric.criterion: Friction notes are specific, not vague
rubric.meets: Each of the five tools has a concrete, specific friction noted — not a general impression like 'clunky.'

rubric.criterion: The structural-versus-taste sort is honest
rubric.meets: At least one gap is honestly categorized as taste rather than inflated into structural, if that's what the evidence actually shows.

rubric.criterion: The differentiation statement (if any) is checkable
rubric.meets: One sentence naming the specific audience, the paid gap, and the free tool's specific barrier — not a vibe about being better.

rubric.criterion: An honest kill, if reached, is treated as a real result
rubric.meets: If no real gap survived, the assessment says so plainly, rather than being stretched to justify building anyway.

contentSections.body: A checkable differentiation sentence, or an honest 'no real gap' — both are real, useful outcomes of this lab, and only one of them means you shouldn't build.

title: Checkpoint — What Already Exists
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from the previous one, two from further back. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's and earlier modules' core distinctions without looking them up

questions.from: This module — What Already Exists
questions.prompt: Why does a generic category search often fail to find real competitors to a niche idea?

options.label: It surfaces well-funded generic competitors and misses niche ones that a specific, audience-language search would find
Search engines don't index niche products at all
Niche competitors deliberately hide from search engines

questions.explanation: A generic term like "habit tracker app" surfaces the biggest, most generic players. Searching with the specific audience's own language, and checking their specific communities, is what finds the niche competitors closest to your actual idea.

questions.from: This module — What Already Exists
questions.prompt: Someone says an existing tool is "just not quite right." What should you do?

options.label: Ask what specifically happens when they try to use it, to find the real structural gap
Accept it as sufficient evidence of a real gap
Move on, since vague dissatisfaction isn't useful

questions.explanation: "Not quite right" is a starting point, not a finding — one good follow-up question usually turns it into something specific and structural, or reveals it's really just a taste mismatch.

questions.from: This module — What Already Exists
questions.prompt: Why doesn't "it's free" automatically mean "it's not real competition"?

options.label: Free tools are still genuine competition unless there's a specific reason your audience can't or won't use them
Free tools are always technically inferior to paid ones
Free tools don't count because nobody trusts them

questions.explanation: The honest question is why the free tool hasn't already won, given that it's free — sometimes it's a real structural barrier for your specific audience, sometimes it's discoverability, and sometimes the free tool genuinely already closes the gap.

questions.from: This module — What Already Exists
questions.prompt: What makes a differentiation statement checkable rather than a vibe?

options.label: It names the specific audience, what paid options assume, and what the free option requires that the audience doesn't have
It uses confident, persuasive language
It's short enough to fit on a slide

questions.explanation: "Better than the competition" is unfalsifiable. A statement built from a specific audience, a specific gap in paid options, and a specific barrier in the free option is something someone else could actually verify or dispute.

questions.from: This module — What Already Exists
questions.prompt: "The market is big enough that there's room for another one" is an example of what?

options.label: A rationalization that doesn't name a specific gap for a specific audience
A strong, defensible business reason to build
Evidence gathered from real competitor research

questions.explanation: This reasoning would apply to almost any idea in almost any market, regardless of what real research found — that's the tell of a rationalization rather than a checkable claim about a specific gap.

questions.from: This module — What Already Exists
questions.prompt: Is it acceptable to build a tool purely to practice a technology, even with no real competitive gap?

options.label: Yes, as long as you're honest that it's a learning project, not a validated market claim
No, every idea has to survive competitive research to be worth building
Yes, and it should still be described to others as a validated gap

questions.explanation: The problem was never building for personal reasons — it's dressing up a personal reason as a market finding the research didn't actually support. Honesty about which kind of reason it is is what separates a legitimate choice from a rationalization.

questions.from: This module — What Already Exists
questions.prompt: A free tool requires editing a config file to set up. Your defined audience is explicitly non-technical. What does this represent?

options.label: A real, structural barrier that makes the free tool effectively unavailable to this specific audience
A minor issue not worth considering, since the tool is free
Proof the free tool is technically inferior

questions.explanation: "Free" only means "available" if the audience can get through the setup — a real technical barrier for a non-technical audience is a structural gap, even though the tool costs nothing in dollars.

questions.from: This module — What Already Exists
questions.prompt: You honestly conclude there's no real gap for your idea. What's the recommended next move?

options.label: Treat it as a good, cheap result, log the finding, and check for any new lead mentioned during the research
Build it anyway, since you've already done the work to get this far
Keep searching until you find a way to justify a gap

questions.explanation: This mirrors the validation-kill lesson from module two — an honest 'no' at this late stage is still far cheaper than building something with no real reason to exist, and it often hands you the next candidate on the way out.

questions.from: The previous module — Who It's For
questions.prompt: What makes a user description actually useful for design decisions?

options.label: Checkable facts — current behavior, device, frequency, a real failure — not adjectives about how the person feels
A realistic-sounding name and a stock photo
Being as long and detailed as possible

questions.explanation: The same checkable-facts standard this module applies to differentiation claims — a description built from real behavior settles arguments; adjectives about feeling don't.

questions.from: Cutting It Down to Shippable
questions.prompt: How do you decide which items on a feature list are required for v1?

options.label: Ask whether the one job still works without it — if yes, defer it; if no, it's required
Keep whichever features are easiest to build
Keep whichever features you personally find most exciting

questions.explanation: The cut test runs off whether the one job breaks without the feature — the same checkable, evidence-based instinct this module uses to sort a real structural gap from a rationalization.
